tree.name: Brown Algae
tree.quizClue: A pair of long wavy blades trailing from a rooted base underwater, more like a flexible ribbon than a leaf.
tree.quizWhy: Brown algae aren't true plants at all — this group includes the kelp forests that form some of the most productive ecosystems in the ocean.

families.name: Laminariaceae
families.trait: Long, smooth, undivided blades growing from a holdfast anchored to rock, with a flexible stipe that lets the blade sway rather than snap in strong currents; among the fastest-growing organisms on Earth.
families.differentia: The classic smooth-bladed kelp — unlike Alariaceae's deeply lobed blade with its distinct basal reproductive frill, or Sargassaceae's branching stem strung with round gas-filled floats.

funFacts.text: Blades reach up to 2 meters long, growing from a branching, finger-like holdfast gripping rock in the low intertidal zone.
Doesn't pollinate at all — it reproduces via microscopic spores released into the water, alternating between a large visible generation and a tiny thread-like one.
Common on rocky Atlantic coastlines from Portugal north to Norway and across to Nova Scotia.
The base of dashi broth, and also cured into tsukudani or eaten pickled.
Traditionally given as a Japanese wedding gift — "kobu" puns with "yorokobu," meaning to rejoice.
Native to the cold coastal waters of Hokkaido and the Sea of Japan, now cultivated across the Asian Pacific coast.
Dominant on cold-temperate rocky coastlines of the North Pacific and North Atlantic, from the low intertidal zone down to about 30 meters.
Dried and simmered to make dashi, the savory stock base of much of Japanese cooking.

families.name: Alariaceae
families.trait: A single blade deeply divided into paired lobes along a central rib (pinnatifid), with a distinct frilly, ruffled cluster of reproductive tissue at the base of the stipe.
families.differentia: Distinguished from Laminariaceae's smooth undivided blade by deep pinnate lobing along a midrib, and from Sargassaceae by lacking any gas-filled floats — buoyancy instead comes from the thin, flexible blade itself.

funFacts.text: A staple in miso soup and seaweed salad.
Native to the coasts of Japan, Korea, and China; now considered invasive in parts of the Mediterranean, California, and Australia after spreading via ship hulls.
Featured in traditional Japanese postpartum diets, where it's believed — though not clinically established — to support recovery.
Wakame beds provide nursery habitat for juvenile fish, sheltering them from predators and current.

families.name: Sargassaceae
families.trait: Bushy, branching thalli bearing small leaf-like blades alongside round, gas-filled bladders (pneumatocysts) that hold the plant upright in the water column.
families.differentia: The only family here with round gas-filled floats studding a branching stem — a buoyancy strategy neither Laminariaceae's rigid stipe nor Alariaceae's flexible blade relies on.

funFacts.text: Simmered with soy sauce and root vegetables in hijiki no nimono, a classic Japanese side dish.
Native to rocky coastlines across Japan, Korea, and China.
Naturally accumulates high levels of inorganic arsenic, which is why Japan, the UK, and Canada advise eating it only in moderation.
Floating Sargassum mats in the open Sargasso Sea shelter eel larvae, juvenile turtles, and the sargassumfish, a predator so well camouflaged it's nearly invisible against the algae.

tree.desc: Large marine algae forming some of the ocean's most productive ecosystems, from smooth-bladed kelp forests to branching, float-buoyed Sargassum mats — grouped here by shared brown pigmentation (fucoxanthin) rather than close evolutionary relationship, since "brown algae" spans multiple real algal orders.

funFacts.text: Found along cold, nutrient-rich coastlines worldwide, forming dense kelp forests especially along the Pacific Rim and North Atlantic.
Kelp forests shelter sea otters, urchins, and hundreds of fish species — otters keep urchin grazing in check, since unchecked urchins can strip a forest into a barren.
Not true plants and have no roots, stems, or leaves at all — a holdfast anchors them to rock, but doesn't draw up water or nutrients the way a root does.

In 2024, paleobiologist Cindy Looy and colleagues dated fossilized kelp holdfasts collected by amateur fossil hunter James Goedert near Jansen Creek, Washington State, to about 32 million years old — more than doubling the previous oldest known kelp fossil, Julescraneia, described in 1965 from Miocene rocks in California.
Species like kombu and wakame are commercially farmed rather than wild-harvested, grown on ropes suspended in coastal waters where they can be lowered to depth and hauled back up again at harvest.

tree.name: Red Algae
tree.quizClue: A branching frond built from repeated forked segments, more delicate and finely divided than a typical broad seaweed blade.
tree.quizWhy: Red algae get their color from phycoerythrin, a pigment that lets them photosynthesize efficiently in deep water where blue light dominates and red light barely penetrates.
tree.desc: Mostly marine algae colored by phycoerythrin rather than chlorophyll alone, ranging from paper-thin edible sheets to finely branched, cartilaginous fronds prized for the gelling agents extracted from their cell walls.

families.name: Bangiaceae
families.trait: Simple, flat, membranous blades only one or two cells thick, growing directly from a small holdfast; the thinness lets light pass almost straight through the living sheet.
families.differentia: The order's flat-sheet specialist — a papery, translucent blade unlike Palmariaceae's lobed hand-shaped frond or Gelidiaceae's fine, repeatedly forking branches.

funFacts.text: Pressed into the thin sheets used to wrap sushi and onigiri.

Modern nori farming exists because British phycologist Kathleen Drew-Baker discovered its hidden shell-boring life stage in 1949 — she's honored with a shrine in Uto, Japan, where farmers still hold an annual festival in her memory.
Native to the cold coastal waters of the northwest Pacific around Japan.
Cultivated on nets suspended in shallow coastal waters across Japan, Korea, and China.

families.name: Palmariaceae
families.trait: A tough, leathery frond that divides into broad, rounded, finger-like lobes fanning out from a narrow stalk, resembling an open hand.
families.differentia: Distinguished from Bangiaceae's flat undivided sheet by a thick, hand-shaped frond split into rounded lobes, and from Gelidiaceae by lacking any fine, repeated branching.

funFacts.text: Eaten raw, dried into chewy strips, or fried crisp — nicknamed "sea bacon" in parts of Ireland and Atlantic Canada for the smoky flavor frying brings out.
Traditionally harvested by hand along the coasts of Ireland, Scotland, and Atlantic Canada.
One of the few plant-based foods naturally containing vitamin B12, though usually not in high enough amounts to rely on as a sole source.
Grows attached to rocks and kelp stipes on cold North Atlantic and North Pacific shores.

families.name: Gelidiaceae
families.trait: Small, wiry, cartilaginous fronds that branch repeatedly into fine, feathery tips; cell walls rich in agarose, the gelling compound extracted and purified into agar.
families.differentia: The order's finely branched specialist — repeated forking into hair-thin tips sets it apart from the broad sheet of Bangiaceae and the lobed hand-shape of Palmariaceae.

funFacts.text: The agar it yields has been the standard gel for growing bacteria in petri dishes since the 1880s, after a German microbiologist's wife suggested it as a substitute for gelatin, which many bacteria could digest and liquefy.
Used to set kanten, a firm, glassy Japanese jelly served in both sweet and savory dishes.
Native to warm coastal waters of the western Pacific, especially around Japan and Korea.
Cell walls yield agar, the gelling polysaccharide extracted by boiling and drying the algae.
Get their color from phycoerythrin, a red pigment that masks chlorophyll and lets them absorb blue light penetrating deeper water than other algae can use.
Include Bangiomorpha, a roughly 1.05-billion-year-old fossil red alga that's the oldest known organism with clearly differentiated sexes.

The Bangiomorpha fossil was collected in 1987 by paleobiologist Nicholas Butterfield during Arctic fieldwork on Somerset Island, Nunavut — one of the most remote fossil sites ever to yield a landmark find.
Coralline red algae cement themselves with calcium carbonate and help build and stabilize coral reef structures, filling gaps between corals like living mortar.

tree.name: Green Algae
tree.quizClue: A single simple stalk splitting into two thin forking tips near the top, with no obvious leaf shape at all.
tree.quizWhy: Green algae share the same chlorophyll pigments as land plants and are their closest living relatives among the algae — all land plants evolved from within this group.
tree.desc: Photosynthetic algae sharing the same chlorophyll a/b pigments as land plants — their closest living relatives among the algae — ranging from paper-thin sheets to bead-strung runners to spongy branching fingers.

families.name: Ulvaceae
families.trait: A thin, bright green, ruffled sheet only two cells thick, growing attached to rocks in the intertidal zone; edible and fast-growing.
families.differentia: The order's flat-sheet family — a ruffled, translucent blade unlike Caulerpaceae's bead-strung runners or Codiaceae's spongy branching fingers.

funFacts.text: Eaten raw in salads or added to soups for a mild, briny flavor.
Grows on rocky shores worldwide, from temperate coastlines to the tropics.
Its blade is only two cells thick, letting it photosynthesize efficiently but also making it especially prone to bloom quickly when conditions favor it.
Can bloom explosively into thick mats called "green tides" when coastal waters carry excess nutrient runoff, sometimes smothering beaches and starving the water of oxygen as the mats decay.

families.name: Caulerpaceae
families.trait: A creeping runner (stolon) sending up clusters of small round, grape-like beads; despite the complex branching shape, the entire plant is a single giant multinucleate cell.
families.differentia: Unmistakable for its bead-like clusters on a creeping stolon, unlike the flat sheet of Ulvaceae or the spongy fingers of Codiaceae.

funFacts.text: Eaten raw with a vinegar dressing; nicknamed "green caviar" for the way its tiny fluid-filled beads pop in the mouth.
Native to the Indo-Pacific, and widely farmed in the Philippines and Okinawa.
A single frond is one giant cell with thousands of nuclei and no internal cell walls — despite looking like a small leafy plant, it's technically unicellular.

families.name: Codiaceae
families.trait: Dense, spongy, velvety tubular branches forking repeatedly from a single holdfast, built from tightly interwoven filaments rather than true tissue.
families.differentia: The order's only family with a spongy, three-dimensional branching “finger” growth form, unlike the flat sheets of Ulvaceae or the bead clusters of Caulerpaceae.

funFacts.text: Native to the Pacific coasts of Japan and Korea.
Introduced along the Atlantic coast of North America, where it grows over oyster and scallop beds and can interfere with shellfish aquaculture.
Nicknamed "dead man's fingers" for its spongy, velvety, finger-like branching fronds.
Use the same chlorophyll a and b as land plants — genetic evidence points to green algae as the ancestral group land plants evolved from.
Found in both marine and freshwater habitats, unlike most brown and red algae, which are almost entirely marine.

In 2020, Virginia Tech postdoctoral researcher Qing Tang identified over 1,000 fossil specimens of Proterocladus antiquus in billion-year-old rocks near Dalian, Liaoning Province, China — the oldest confirmed green algae fossil, pushing back the record for green plant life by roughly 200 million years.

tree.name: Bryophytes
tree.quizClue: Three short upright stalks of slightly different heights, each capped with a small oval knob, clustered together in a tuft.
tree.quizWhy: Bryophytes were among the first plants to colonize land and lack true vascular tissue, so most stay low to the ground and absorb water directly through their surfaces.
tree.desc: A grouping of three separate, non-vascular land-plant lineages — mosses, liverworts, and hornworts — among the earliest plants to colonize land, reproducing by spores rather than seeds and lacking the internal plumbing of later plants.

families.name: Sphagnaceae
families.trait: Dense, spongy cushions of tightly packed stems, each topped with a star-shaped cluster of branches; dead tissue below can hold up to twenty times its weight in water.
families.differentia: The order's most economically significant family, forming vast waterlogged peat bogs, unlike the flat thalloid growth of Marchantiaceae or the horn-shaped capsule of Anthocerotaceae.

funFacts.text: Used as wound dressing in World War I field hospitals — its acidic, absorbent tissue is mildly antibacterial and can hold far more fluid than cotton gauze.
Accumulates into peat so slowly that peatlands, though covering only a few percent of Earth's land, store more carbon than all the world's forests combined.
Forms vast peat bogs across cold, wet regions of the Northern Hemisphere.
Can hold up to 20 times its dry weight in water within specialized dead cells, which is why peat bogs stay waterlogged.

families.name: Marchantiaceae
families.trait: A flat, forking, ribbon-like body (thallus) pressed against damp soil or rock, lacking distinct stems or leaves; reproduces via small umbrella-shaped stalked structures.
families.differentia: Distinguished from Sphagnum's upright, needle-leaved stems by a completely flat, leafless ribbon body, and from Anthocerotaceae by lacking a horn-shaped spore capsule.

funFacts.text: Reproduces asexually via tiny cup-shaped structures called gemmae cups, which splash their contents out when struck by falling raindrops.
A widespread weed of damp soil, greenhouse pots, and disturbed ground worldwide.
Named under the old "Doctrine of Signatures" — its flat, lobed, liver-shaped thallus led herbalists to believe it could treat liver ailments, hence "liverwort."

families.name: Anthocerotaceae
families.trait: A small, flat, lobed thallus similar to a liverwort, topped by a single tall, tapering, horn-shaped spore capsule that splits open from the tip as it releases spores.
families.differentia: Unmistakable for its tall, horn-shaped spore capsule rising straight up from a flat thallus, unlike the umbrella-topped Marchantiaceae or upright leafy Sphagnaceae.

funFacts.text: Each cell contains a single large chloroplast, unlike nearly every other land plant, whose cells hold many small ones — a trait shared with algae.
Often one of the first plants to colonize bare, disturbed, damp soil in temperate regions.
Hosts colonies of nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria inside internal mucilage-filled cavities — an internal microbial partnership rare among plants.
Don't pollinate — they reproduce via spores, and their sperm cells need a film of water to physically swim to an egg, which is why bryophytes stay small and low to the ground.
The first land plants lacked true roots, stems, or vascular tissue, so water and nutrients move by simple diffusion — a major limit on how tall they can grow.

In 2007, paleobotanist Linda VanAller Hernick and colleagues described Metzgeriothallus sharonae, the oldest known liverwort fossil, from Middle Devonian shale (roughly 383 million years old) near Cairo, New York — the specimens included the first fossil evidence of a liverwort reproductive structure.

tree.name: Ferns
tree.quizClue: A tall central stalk with paired side-branches alternating up its length, curling into a small spiral at the very tip.
tree.quizWhy: Ferns reproduce by spores rather than seeds, and new fronds famously emerge tightly coiled into a spiral called a fiddlehead before unfurling.
tree.desc: Seedless vascular plants reproducing by spores, spanning finely divided true ferns and their ancient horsetail relatives — among the first plants to evolve true vascular tissue, allowing them to grow larger and colonize drier ground than mosses and liverworts.

families.name: Nephrolepidaceae
families.trait: Long, gracefully arching fronds densely packed with many small, narrow leaflets along the entire length of the stalk; spreads via wiry runners and small water-storing tubers.
families.differentia: Distinguished from Polypodiaceae's simple, undivided fronds by finely divided, densely packed leaflets running the full length of the frond.

funFacts.text: The "Boston" name comes from a mutant, extra-frilly frond variety discovered in a Boston shipment in 1894, which set off a Victorian houseplant fad.
One of the houseplants tested in NASA's Clean Air Study for removing indoor pollutants like formaldehyde from the air.
Native to tropical regions including Florida, the Caribbean, and parts of Africa and Asia.
Native to tropical and subtropical regions worldwide.

families.name: Polypodiaceae
families.trait: Two distinct frond types on one plant: flat, round “shield” fronds that clasp the host tree, and upright, repeatedly forking, antler-shaped fertile fronds; grows epiphytically on bark rather than rooted in soil.
families.differentia: The order's only epiphytic family with antler-shaped, forking fronds, unlike the finely pinnate fronds of Nephrolepidaceae or the jointed stems of Equisetaceae.

funFacts.text: Grows two distinct frond types: flat sterile "shield" fronds that clasp the host tree and catch falling debris as natural fertilizer, and forked, antler-shaped fertile fronds that bear the spores.
Grows harmlessly on tree trunks and branches, taking no nutrients from its host — a passenger, not a parasite.
Native to the rainforests of eastern Australia and New Guinea.
Many members are epiphytic, growing on tree bark and branches rather than in soil.

families.name: Equisetaceae
families.trait: Hollow, jointed, ribbed stems reinforced with silica, with whorls of thin needle-like side branches emerging at each node; an ancient lineage that once included forest-sized trees.
families.differentia: Immediately recognizable by its jointed, bamboo-like segmented stem, unlike the divided fronds of Nephrolepidaceae and Polypodiaceae — technically a “fern ally” rather than a true fern, but conventionally grouped with ferns.

funFacts.text: Stems are packed with abrasive silica, and were historically bundled and used to scour pots and polish pewter — hence the common name "scouring rush."
Used in traditional herbal medicine as a diuretic, though clinical evidence for this effect remains limited.
A "fern ally," not a true fern — horsetails split off onto their own ancient lineage long before modern ferns diversified, though they're often shown alongside ferns since both reproduce by spores.
Never flower or pollinate — they reproduce via spores released from clusters on the underside of fronds.
Fern-dominated forests covered much of Earth around 300 million years ago; their compressed remains form a large share of the world's coal deposits.

In 2014, researchers Benjamin Bomfleur, Stephen McLoughlin, and Vivi Vajda described a 180-million-year-old royal fern (Osmundaceae) fossil from Korsaröd, Sweden, so rapidly buried by a volcanic mudflow that intact cell nuclei and chromosomes were preserved — showing the fern's genome size had stayed essentially unchanged for 180 million years.

children.name: Ginkgoales
children.quizClue: A fan-shaped leaf with a shallow notch splitting its outer edge into two lobes, and thin veins radiating up from the base — the same silhouette used on Tokyo's civic emblem.
children.quizWhy: Ginkgo biloba is the only living species in this order, and its fan-shaped leaf with a central notch is one of the most recognizable leaf outlines in the plant kingdom.

families.name: Ginkgoaceae
families.trait: A single living species, Ginkgo biloba, with fan-shaped leaves showing a distinctive central notch and forked (dichotomous) venation unlike any other tree; separate male and female trees, the female producing foul-smelling but historically prized seeds.
families.differentia: The order's only family and one of the most ancient lineages in the plant kingdom — a living fossil essentially unchanged for over 200 million years.

funFacts.text: Often called a "living fossil" — fossils of trees essentially identical to modern Ginkgo biloba date back over 200 million years, predating most dinosaurs.
Six ginkgo trees growing within one to two kilometers of the Hiroshima atomic bomb hypocenter survived the blast and are still alive today.
The sole surviving species of an entire lineage that has remained essentially unchanged in the fossil record for over 200 million years, earning it the nickname "living fossil."
Several ginkgo trees growing within a mile or two of the 1945 Hiroshima atomic bomb hypocenter survived and are still alive today, now honored locally as symbols of resilience.

A dioecious species — female trees produce seeds surrounded by a fleshy coating that smells strongly of rancid butter as it decomposes, which is why male trees are almost always chosen for street planting.

children.desc: A single living species order — the most ancient surviving seed-plant lineage, essentially unchanged in the fossil record for over 200 million years.

children.name: Pinales
children.quizClue: A stack of triangles narrowing toward the top on a short trunk — the generic pine-tree silhouette.
children.quizWhy: This order contains essentially all living conifers, so a simple pine-tree silhouette can stand in for the whole group.

families.name: Pinaceae
families.trait: Needle-like leaves borne singly or in bundles of two to five; large woody cones with overlapping scales, and resin canals running through the wood.
families.differentia: The order's largest family by far — distinguished from Cupressaceae by true needle leaves (not scale-like) and by cones with separate, overlapping woody scales rather than fused or berry-like ones.

funFacts.text: Typically grows 20–35 m tall, with some old individuals in Scandinavia exceeding 40 m.
The most widely distributed pine species in the world, ranging from western Europe across Siberia to the Pacific coast of Russia.
Young pollen cones and inner bark have been used historically in Scandinavia and Russia as a famine food and flavoring.
The traditional Christmas tree of much of central Europe before the Norway spruce and Nordmann fir became more common commercially.
Can exceed 50 m, making it one of the tallest tree species native to Europe.

Old Tjikko, a Norway spruce on Fulufjället Mountain in Sweden, was identified in 2004 by physical geographer Leif Kullman, who carbon-dated its root system to about 9,550 years old — the oldest known individual of the species, though its visible trunk is only a few centuries old.
The classic European Christmas tree, and the species behind the giant tree presented annually in London's Trafalgar Square as a gift from Norway since 1947.
Appears on the flag and coat of arms of Lebanon, and its timber was prized in antiquity for shipbuilding and temple construction, including the Temple of Solomon.
Surviving old-growth groves are now restricted to a few protected sites in Lebanon's mountains, most famously the "Cedars of God," after centuries of logging.
Dominant across the cool and boreal forests of the Northern Hemisphere, from the Arctic treeline down through temperate mountain ranges.

families.name: Cupressaceae
families.trait: Small, scale-like or awl-shaped leaves pressed flat against the twig; cones either small and woody or, in junipers, fused into fleshy blue “berries.”
families.differentia: Unlike Pinaceae's needle bundles and separate-scaled cones, this family's leaves hug the stem in flattened sprays, and its cones can fuse into soft, berry-like structures instead of staying woody.

funFacts.text: Has the largest natural geographic range of any woody plant species in the world, spanning the cool temperate Northern Hemisphere from Alaska to Japan.
Its berry-like cones flavor gin — the drink's name traces back through Dutch "jenever" and French "genièvre," both meaning juniper.
The tallest tree species on Earth — the current record holder, Hyperion, stands over 115 m (379 ft) tall.

Hyperion was found in August 2006 by naturalists Chris Atkins and Michael Taylor while exploring a remote section of Redwood National Park, California; its height was confirmed days later by ecologist Stephen Sillett, who climbed to the top and dropped a tape measure to the ground.
Protected by bark up to 30 cm thick that resists both fire and insect damage, letting individual trees live over 2,000 years.
Includes both the tallest trees on Earth (coast redwood) and some of the most cold-hardy, low-growing conifers (juniper) — an unusually wide range of forms for one family.

children.desc: The living conifers — evergreen, resin-producing trees and shrubs bearing seeds in woody cones rather than flowers, with needle- or scale-like leaves adapted to conserve water through harsh winters.

funFacts.text: Wind-pollinated — cones release pollen in enormous clouds rather than relying on animals, a strategy shared by nearly all conifers.
Bear "naked" seeds sitting exposed on cone scales rather than enclosed in a fruit — the literal meaning of "gymnosperm."

children.name: Amborellales
children.quizClue: A small, unremarkable shrub outline with two tiny round berries perched at the tips of its twigs.
children.quizWhy: Amborella trichopoda, the order's only species, is an inconspicuous woody shrub — often cited as the single earliest-diverging lineage of all living flowering plants.

families.name: Amborellaceae
families.trait: A single living species, Amborella trichopoda, an inconspicuous woody shrub native only to New Caledonia, most notable for its position at the very base of the flowering-plant family tree rather than any visible trait.
families.differentia: The order's only family, and by most molecular analyses the single earliest-diverging lineage of all living flowering plants.

funFacts.text: Contains a single living species, found only in the understory forests of New Caledonia, that most phylogenetic analyses place as the earliest-diverging lineage among all living flowering plants.

Its unique evolutionary position wasn't confirmed until DNA-based phylogenetic studies in the 1990s and 2000s untangled the base of the flowering-plant family tree — before molecular data, its significance as a living relic of the earliest angiosperms wasn't recognized.

children.desc: A single-species order occupying, by most analyses, the earliest-diverging position in the entire flowering-plant family tree.

children.name: Nymphaeales
children.quizClue: A flat oval pad floating below a teardrop bud rising up out of the water.
children.quizWhy: This order is the water lilies — aquatic plants with floating pads and flowers that rise up above the water's surface.

families.name: Nymphaeaceae
families.trait: Aquatic perennials with round, waxy floating leaves and showy flowers that open at or just above the water's surface; among the most ancient surviving flowering-plant lineages, retaining relatively primitive floral structure.
families.differentia: The order's defining family — true water lilies, floating rather than emergent like the unrelated lotus (Nelumbonaceae) elsewhere in the Diagram.

funFacts.text: Water lilies sit near the very base of the flowering-plant family tree, making them one of the most ancient living lineages of flowering plants.
Many water lily flowers open in the morning and close again at night, repeating the cycle over several days before the bloom finally fades.
Among the most ancient surviving lineages of flowering plants, with a fossil record stretching back over 100 million years.
Their floating leaves have a waxy upper surface and stomata (pores) only on top, an adaptation unique among most plants, whose pores are usually on the underside where water loss is minimized.

children.desc: The water lilies — aquatic perennials with floating leaves and flowers, among the most ancient surviving lineages of flowering plants.

children.name: Austrobaileyales
children.quizClue: Eight thin boat-shaped pods radiating from a central hub, like a dried spice pod split open into a star.
children.quizWhy: This order includes Illiciaceae, the family that produces star anise, whose dried fruit is a star-shaped ring of pointed pods.

families.name: Schisandraceae
families.trait: Star-shaped, many-chambered dry fruit that splits open into boat-shaped pods; primitive flowers with numerous spirally arranged tepals and stamens.
families.differentia: The order's only economically important family — its dry, star-shaped fruit is unlike anything else among the basal angiosperm lineages nearby in the Diagram.

funFacts.text: A core spice in Chinese five-spice powder and Vietnamese pho broth, prized for its warm, licorice-like flavor.
Its shikimic acid was, for years, the primary industrial starting material for synthesizing the antiviral drug oseltamivir (Tamiflu).

A toxic look-alike, Japanese star anise (Illicium anisatum), can contaminate poorly regulated supplies and has caused poisoning outbreaks, which is why star anise is subject to import screening in some countries.
One of the earliest-diverging lineages of flowering plants, branching off near the base of the angiosperm family tree.

children.desc: A small, ancient order of woody plants retaining primitive floral traits from near the base of the flowering-plant family tree, most familiar through the star-shaped dried fruit of star anise.

children.name: Laurales
children.quizClue: A single long oval leaf on a straight stem — about as plain as a leaf shape gets.
children.quizWhy: This order includes laurel, bay, avocado, and cinnamon — plants best known for simple, aromatic evergreen leaves.

families.name: Lauraceae
families.trait: Simple, leathery, often aromatic evergreen leaves; small flowers in clusters; one-seeded berry or drupe fruits.
families.differentia: The family that gives the order its economic identity — nearly every commercially important Laurales plant, from bay leaves to avocado to cinnamon bark, belongs here.

funFacts.text: Botanically a single-seeded berry, not a vegetable.

Its oversized seed and rich pulp are cited as a likely example of an "evolutionary anachronism" — a fruit shaped to be swallowed whole by now-extinct Ice Age megafauna like ground sloths and gomphotheres, whose disappearance left the avocado without its original seed disperser.
Native to south-central Mexico, where it was domesticated thousands of years ago.
"True" or Ceylon cinnamon, distinct from the stronger, cheaper cassia (Cinnamomum cassia) more commonly sold as "cinnamon" in North America.
Native to Sri Lanka, historically called Ceylon, which remains the world's main source of true cinnamon.
Traded along ancient spice routes for millennia and mentioned in Egyptian, Hebrew, and Greek texts as a luxury good used in incense and embalming.
Harvested by coppicing - cutting the stems back to encourage new shoots - then peeling the inner bark from those young shoots, which curls into quills as it dries.
Victors in ancient Greece and Rome were crowned with wreaths of bay laurel leaves — the origin of terms like "poet laureate" and "baccalaureate."
Dried whole, its leaves are simmered in stews and sauces for their aroma, then almost always fished back out before serving — the leaf itself is tough and unpleasant to eat.
Leaves are hand-picked year-round from mature shrubs and air-dried out of direct sun, which preserves their aroma better than fast drying.

children.desc: Aromatic evergreen trees and shrubs with simple, leathery leaves and small flowers borne in clusters, prized worldwide for the essential oils concentrated in their bark and leaves.

children.name: Magnoliales
children.quizClue: A closed teardrop-shaped bud with a couple of curved lines peeking out from behind it, as if petals are still wrapped shut.
children.quizWhy: Magnolia flowers are famous for opening from a large, tightly wrapped closed bud with overlapping tepals.

families.name: Myristicaceae
families.trait: Aromatic seeds enclosed in a fleshy fruit that splits to reveal a bright red, lacy aril wrapped around the true seed within.
families.differentia: The order's only family represented here — unique for yielding two distinct spices (nutmeg the seed, mace the lacy aril) from a single fruit.

funFacts.text: Produces two separate spices from one fruit: nutmeg is the seed itself, while mace is the bright red, lacy covering (aril) wrapped around it.

Native only to Indonesia's Banda Islands, where its rarity fueled such fierce colonial competition that in 1667 the Dutch traded the island of Manhattan to England for full control of a single tiny nutmeg-growing island, Run.
Contains myristicin, a compound that is toxic and mildly hallucinogenic in large doses — a few whole nutmegs can cause serious poisoning.

The fruit is split open at harvest to reveal a seed wrapped in a lacy red aril; the aril is peeled off and dried separately to become mace, while the seed itself is dried for weeks before cracking to yield the nutmeg.

families.name: Magnoliaceae
families.trait: Large, often fragrant flowers that open from a tightly wrapped, torpedo-shaped bud into big waxy tepals arranged in an overlapping spiral rather than distinct whorls of petals and sepals; an ancient lineage that evolved before bees, originally pollinated by beetles.
families.differentia: The order's namesake family and its only broadly cultivated ornamental — its large spiral-tepaled flowers stand apart from Myristicaceae's inconspicuous blooms, hidden inside an aril-wrapped fruit.

funFacts.text: Magnolias are considered one of the most primitive living flowering-plant lineages — their flowers evolved before bees existed, which is why many species are still pollinated by beetles rather than bees.
Its tough, waxy petals evolved to withstand being crawled over by beetles, the flower's original pollinators, long before bees existed to do the job more gently.
Native to the southeastern United States, it has since become one of the most widely planted ornamental trees in warm climates worldwide.

children.desc: Woody trees and shrubs with large, often solitary flowers and numerous spirally arranged floral parts, an early-diverging lineage that predates the split between monocots and eudicots.

children.name: Piperales
children.quizClue: A thin stem topped by a tall narrow capsule, like a catkin or a dense flower spike.
children.quizWhy: Peppercorns form on a dense, elongated flower spike — this is the plant family behind black pepper.

families.name: Piperaceae
families.trait: Jointed, often swollen stem nodes; tiny flowers lacking petals, packed densely onto a narrow upright or hanging spike; many species rich in pungent alkaloids.
families.differentia: The order's defining family — black pepper's dense flower spike and pungent alkaloid chemistry (piperine) are unique to this lineage among the early-diverging angiosperms nearby in the Diagram.

funFacts.text: Black, white, and green peppercorns can all come from the very same plant — the difference is simply when the berry is picked and how it is processed afterward.
Pepper was so valuable in medieval Europe that it was sometimes used to pay rent, taxes, or dowries, and hoarded merchant wealth was literally measured "by the peppercorn."

Grown as a vine trained up a support pole; unripe berries are hand-picked and dried in the sun to make black peppercorns, while fully ripe berries are soaked to remove the skin before drying into white pepper.
The source of black, white, and green peppercorns — all three come from the same species, Piper nigrum, differing only in when the fruit is picked and how it's processed.
Black pepper was so valuable in medieval Europe that it was sometimes used as currency and collateral for loans, part of the spice trade that helped motivate the Age of Exploration.

children.desc: Herbs, shrubs, and vines with jointed stems and tiny flowers packed onto dense spikes, source of the world's most widely traded spice, black pepper.

children.name: Liliales
children.quizClue: Two curved trumpet shapes meeting at a single stem.
children.quizWhy: This order includes true lilies and tulips, known for large trumpet- or bell-shaped flowers with six tepals.

families.name: Liliaceae
families.trait: Six-parted, often trumpet- or bell-shaped flowers with parallel-veined leaves; most grow from a true bulb that persists underground between seasons.
families.differentia: The order's namesake and best-known family — its large, six-tepaled bulb flowers define the classic lily-and-tulip silhouette that gives Liliales its name.

funFacts.text: Central to "tulip mania" in the Dutch Republic during the 1630s, when bulb prices for rare varieties briefly exceeded the price of houses — often cited as one of history's first recorded speculative market bubbles.
Despite its strong association with the Netherlands, the genus originated in Central Asia and was first cultivated in Ottoman Turkey before reaching Europe in the 16th century.
One of the oldest cultivated flowers in history, depicted in Minoan frescoes on Crete over 3,000 years ago, and later adopted in Christian art as a symbol of purity associated with the Virgin Mary.
Native to the Balkans and the eastern Mediterranean, unlike most garden lily hybrids today, which descend mainly from East Asian species.

Bulbs are planted shallowly in late summer, since (unlike a tulip's papery tunic) they have no protective outer skin and dry out if left exposed; established clumps are dug up and divided every few years as the bulbs multiply into offsets.

children.desc: Mostly bulb-forming perennial herbs with six-parted, often large and showy flowers displaying parallel venation — the archetypal lily-and-tulip look of early spring gardens.

children.name: Asparagales
children.icon: <ellipse cx="20" cy="18" rx="10" ry="6"/><path d="M20 24v10"/><ellipse cx="20" cy="14" rx="3" ry="5"/>
children.quizClue: A wide flattened oval bloom perched on a thin stalk.
children.quizWhy: This order spans orchids, onions, and asparagus — a huge, morphologically diverse monocot group united more by genetics than by one visible trait.

families.name: Amaryllidaceae
families.trait: Bulb-forming perennials with strap-shaped leaves and flowers clustered in an umbel beneath a papery bract; many concentrate pungent sulfur compounds in the bulb.
families.differentia: Unlike Iridaceae's fused three-plus-three tepals or Orchidaceae's single asymmetric lip, this family bundles its flowers into an umbel under a papery spathe, and several members (onion, garlic, leek) store pungent sulfur compounds in their bulbs.

funFacts.text: The national flower of Wales, traditionally worn on St. David's Day.
All parts of the plant, especially the bulb, contain lycorine, and daffodil bulbs are occasionally mistaken for onions in gardens — a mix-up that causes plant poisoning cases most years.
The other national emblem of Wales, alongside the daffodil — legend holds that St. David told Welsh soldiers to wear leeks in their helmets to tell themselves apart from Saxon enemies in battle.
Cutting an onion ruptures cells and releases a volatile sulfur compound, syn-propanethial-S-oxide, that irritates the eyes and triggers tears on contact.
Domesticated more than 5,000 years ago, making it one of the oldest continuously cultivated vegetables.
Grown from seed, seedlings, or small bulbs called "sets"; harvested once the leafy tops yellow and fall over, then cured in a dry, airy spot for days to weeks so the outer skin toughens for storage.
Used as a folk remedy in ancient Egypt — the Greek historian Herodotus recorded that pyramid laborers were given garlic rations, and cloves have been found among artifacts in Tutankhamun's tomb.
Its pungency comes from allicin, formed only after a clove is crushed or chopped, which triggers a chemical reaction between two compounds normally kept separate in the intact cell.
Propagated by planting individual cloves rather than seed, in autumn in most climates; bulbs are dug up once the leaves begin to brown, then cured and dried before the papery skin is stored intact.

Spans both dinner-table staples (onion, garlic, leek) and toxic ornamentals (daffodil) — nearly all members contain some alkaloid, but only the Allium branch developed the sulfur compounds that make them edible and flavorful rather than poisonous.

families.name: Iridaceae
families.trait: Flowers built from two mirrored sets of three tepals fused at the base into a slender tube; flattened, sword-shaped leaves arranged in a fan.
families.differentia: Distinguished from the bulb-umbels of Amaryllidaceae by fan-shaped, sword-like leaves and a flower built from two whorls of three tepals rather than one true umbel.

funFacts.text: The source of saffron, the world's most expensive spice by weight — each flower yields only three thread-like stigmas, all hand-picked, so roughly 150 flowers are needed to produce a single gram.
A sterile triploid that can no longer produce viable seeds; every saffron crocus in cultivation is propagated by hand-dividing its underground corms.
Each corm produces just a few flowers, and the three red stigmas inside must be hand-picked at dawn before the bloom wilts; roughly 150 flowers yield only a gram of dried saffron.
Named for Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow, reflecting the genus's enormous range of flower colors.

families.name: Orchidaceae
families.trait: Bilaterally symmetric flowers with a single, highly modified lip petal and fused reproductive column; one of the largest flowering-plant families, mostly epiphytic.
families.differentia: The order's most morphologically extreme family here — a bilaterally symmetric flower with one showy lip petal, unlike the radial symmetry of every other Asparagales family in this set.

funFacts.text: The national flower of Indonesia, where it grows wild in humid lowland forests.
Epiphytic in the wild, growing anchored to tree bark rather than rooted in soil, absorbing moisture and nutrients from humid air and rain.
One of the two largest families of flowering plants, with an estimated 28,000 species — roughly 10% of all known flowering plants.
Many species use deceptive pollination, such as bee orchids whose flowers mimic the look and scent of a female bee closely enough to trick males into attempting to mate with them.

families.name: Asparagaceae
families.icon: <ellipse cx="20" cy="18" rx="10" ry="6"/><path d="M20 24v10"/><ellipse cx="20" cy="14" rx="3" ry="5"/>
families.trait: A family broadened by DNA evidence to span succulent rosette shrubs, tender edible shoots, and small bulbous bloomers.
families.differentia: A catch-all reshaped by genetics rather than looks — spans succulent Yucca rosettes, tender Asparagus shoots, and small bulbous Muscari blooms with little in common visually.

funFacts.text: Named for its tight cluster of small, round, blue flowers, which resembles a miniature bunch of grapes.
A dioecious species — individual plants are either male or female, unusual among cultivated vegetables.
Digesting it produces methanethiol, a sulfurous compound that gives urine a distinctive smell afterward; not everyone can smell it, due to genetic variation in odor receptors.

A perennial crop that takes two to three years to establish before the first harvest; young spears are cut by hand just above soil level each spring, and the plant is left to grow into tall fern-like foliage the rest of the season to recharge the roots.

Pollinated exclusively by yucca moths (Tegeticula), in an obligate mutualism where each species depends entirely on the other — the moth is the plant's only pollinator, and its larvae feed only on the resulting seeds.

children.desc: The most diverse monocot order in cultivation, spanning bulb flowers, alliums, orchids, and succulent rosette plants — united more by DNA than by any single shared appearance.

children.name: Pandanales
children.quizClue: A curling fan of leaf blades spiraling outward from one point.
children.quizWhy: Screw pines (Pandanus) have long strap-like leaves that spiral around the stem in a distinctive corkscrew pattern.

families.name: Pandanaceae
families.trait: Long, strap-like leaves arranged in a spiral around the stem, often edged with sharp spines; aerial prop roots support the trunk in some species; separate male and female plants.
families.differentia: The order's defining family — screw pines are named for the distinctive corkscrew spiral in which their strap-like leaves wrap around the stem.

funFacts.text: Sometimes nicknamed "the vanilla of Southeast Asia," a few pandan leaves simmered with rice or desserts impart a sweet, nutty, grassy aroma without any pandan flesh being eaten at all.
Supported above ground by a cone of thick aerial prop roots, an adaptation that helps anchor the plant in the loose, sandy or waterlogged soils of the tropical coastlines it typically grows on.
Several species' leaves are used across Southeast Asian cooking for their distinctive sweet, grassy aroma, sometimes described as tasting like vanilla and coconut combined.

children.desc: Tropical monocots with spirally arranged, often spine-edged strap leaves, commonly propped up by aerial roots.

children.name: Dioscoreales
children.quizClue: A heart-shaped leaf with a curling, twining vine looping beneath it.
children.quizWhy: Yams are twining vines with broad heart-shaped leaves, storing their energy in large underground tubers.

families.name: Dioscoreaceae
families.trait: Twining herbaceous vines with heart-shaped leaves showing networked (reticulate) venation, unusual among monocots; store starch in large underground tubers.
families.differentia: The order's defining family — its net-veined leaves break the parallel-vein rule that holds across nearly every other monocot order in the Diagram.

funFacts.text: A major starch staple across West Africa, the Caribbean, and the Pacific Islands.

Frequently confused with sweet potato in North American grocery stores and recipes, but the two aren't closely related at all — sweet potato belongs to the morning glory family (Convolvulaceae), an entirely different order.

Grown from small tuber pieces planted at the start of the rainy season and trained up stakes or trellises; the mature tubers are dug up by hand months later, which can damage the brittle skin if done carelessly.

children.desc: Mostly twining vines with net-veined leaves (unusual among monocots) that store energy in large underground tubers, cultivated across the tropics as a staple starch crop.

children.name: Alismatales
children.quizClue: A sharply pointed spearhead shape with two flaring barbs at its base.
children.quizWhy: This order includes arrowhead (Sagittaria) and taro, many with sagittate (arrow-shaped) leaves adapted to wet or aquatic habitats.

families.name: Araceae
families.trait: Flowers reduced and densely packed onto a fleshy spike (spadix), often wrapped in a showy modified leaf (spathe); many species carry calcium oxalate crystals that make raw tissue irritating until cooked.
families.differentia: The order's most species-rich and visually distinct family here — the spadix-and-spathe flower cluster sets it apart from every other flower shape in the Diagram's monocot orders.

funFacts.text: Contains sharp calcium oxalate crystals that cause intense irritation if eaten raw — the corms must always be cooked before eating.
One of the oldest cultivated food plants in Southeast Asia and the Pacific, and the base ingredient of Hawaiian poi.

Propagated from the corm's growing tip rather than seed, often grown in flooded paddies like rice; the corms are dug up after 6-12 months and must be cooked before eating, since raw tissue is loaded with irritating calcium oxalate crystals.
Its iconic perforated ("fenestrated") leaves are still debated among botanists — proposed explanations include letting dappled light reach lower leaves and reducing wind damage in storms.
Its fruit takes about a year to ripen and is unsafe to eat before then, due to irritating oxalate crystals that break down only once the fruit fully matures.

children.desc: A largely aquatic and wetland order, from floating-leaved marsh plants to houseplant vines, many bearing tiny flowers packed onto a fleshy spike wrapped in a modified leaf.

children.name: Poales
children.quizClue: A tall thin stem with small diagonal marks along it, like blades of grass.
children.quizWhy: This order is the grasses — wheat, rice, corn, bamboo — all sharing narrow blade-like leaves and wind-pollinated flower spikes.

families.name: Poaceae
families.trait: Hollow, jointed stems (culms) with narrow, parallel-veined leaves sheathing the stem at each node; tiny wind-pollinated flowers clustered into spikelets.
families.differentia: The family that gives the order its name and dominates it by sheer numbers — hollow jointed stems and wind-pollinated spikelets set every grass apart from Bromeliaceae's water-holding leaf rosette.

funFacts.text: The most drought-tolerant of the major cereal crops, making it a staple across Africa's semi-arid Sahel region and parts of India.
Sown at the start of the rainy season in poor, sandy soils where few other grains survive; the seed heads are cut and dried, then threshed and ground into flour.
A dietary staple across much of sub-Saharan Africa, also grown widely for animal feed, sorghum syrup, and biofuel.
Direct-seeded like corn but far more drought-tolerant; grain heads are combine-harvested once mature and threshed, with the stalks sometimes pressed for syrup.

Geneticist George Beadle proposed in the 1930s–40s that corn descended from teosinte, a Mexican wild grass that looks nothing like it; he later bred the two together and calculated that only about five genes account for their dramatic visible differences — a finding later confirmed by DNA analysis and archaeology.
Domesticated from teosinte roughly 9,000 years ago in the Balsas River basin of southwestern Mexico.

Seeds are planted directly in rows after the last frost and cultivated to control weeds while young; harvested once the husks dry and kernels reach a hard, low-moisture stage, then dried further before milling or storage.
A staple food for over half the world's population, more than any other single crop.
Seedlings are started in nurseries and transplanted by hand or machine into flooded paddies; fields are drained before harvest, and the grain is threshed, then milled to remove the husk and bran.
A hexaploid — it carries three complete sets of chromosomes from three different wild grass species, the result of two separate hybridization events roughly 8,000–10,000 years ago.
One of the founding crops of the Fertile Crescent's Neolithic agricultural revolution.
Sown in autumn (winter wheat) or spring and left largely unweeded once established; combine harvesters cut and thresh the ripe grain in one pass, which is then milled into flour.

Uses C4 photosynthesis, a more efficient carbon-fixing pathway than most plants, letting it convert sunlight into biomass unusually quickly — part of why it's grown at massive scale for both sugar and ethanol biofuel.
Propagated from stem cuttings rather than seed; stalks are cut near ground level 12-24 months later and rushed to a mill within hours, since sucrose begins degrading as soon as the cane is cut.
Among the fastest-growing plants on Earth; some bamboo species can grow close to a meter in a single day under ideal conditions.

Many bamboo species flower only once every several decades, with widely dispersed plants of the same clonal origin often flowering in near-perfect synchrony worldwide — a phenomenon still not fully explained.
Gets its citrus scent from citral, despite having no relation to actual citrus plants.
A staple aromatic in Thai and Vietnamese cooking, also used in traditional medicine across South and Southeast Asia.
One of the oldest cultivated cereals in Africa, grown across West Africa for millennia, valued for cooking in as little as five minutes.
Its grains are so tiny — smaller than a grain of sand — that a West African proverb holds it takes real skill and patience to harvest and clean them.
Sown by broadcasting the tiny seed over prepared soil; harvested by hand with sickles, since the fine grain shatters easily, then pounded to remove a tough husk before cooking.

Cereal grains across this family share a common cultivation arc: direct-seeded, largely left to grow once established, then cut and threshed in one pass by a combine harvester, which separates grain from straw and chaff in the same operation.

families.name: Bromeliaceae
families.trait: Rosettes of stiff, often spiny-edged leaves that channel rainwater to a central tank; many species are epiphytic, and the fruit forms from an entire flower spike fusing together.
families.differentia: Unlike the hollow stems and wind-pollinated spikelets of Poaceae, this family holds water in a leaf-rosette tank and fuses a whole flower cluster into one compound fruit — the pineapple.

funFacts.text: Not a single fruit but a "multiple fruit" — it forms from dozens of individual flowers along a central stalk that fuse together as they mature.
Native to South America; Christopher Columbus's crew were among the first Europeans to encounter it, on the island of Guadeloupe in 1493.
Propagated from the leafy crown cut off a harvested fruit rather than from seed; each plant produces a single fruit over 18-24 months, cut by hand once the base of the fruit turns yellow.

children.desc: The wind-pollinated backbone of human agriculture — grasses, cereals, and their bromeliad relatives, defined by reduced, tightly clustered flowers adapted for pollination without insects.

funFacts.text: Almost all grasses are wind-pollinated rather than insect-pollinated, unusual among flowering plants and reflected in their small, petal-less flowers.
Cover roughly one-fifth of Earth's land surface, and this single family supplies the majority of humanity's staple calories through wheat, rice, corn, sorghum, millet, and sugarcane.

children.name: Zingiberales
children.quizClue: Two broad curved fronds arcing away from a central stem, like a banana leaf.
children.quizWhy: Bananas, ginger, and cardamom all belong here, typically with broad paddle-shaped leaves growing from a central stalk.

families.name: Zingiberaceae
families.trait: Aromatic rhizomes packed with essential oils; asymmetric flowers with a single showy petal-like staminode, growing from reed-like pseudostems.
families.differentia: Named for and dominated by its aromatic rhizome spices — ginger and the two cardamoms — unlike Musaceae's starchy, fruit-bearing pseudostem.

funFacts.text: The edible part is a rhizome — an underground stem, not a root.
Used for centuries in traditional Chinese and Ayurvedic medicine to settle nausea, an effect with some modern clinical support.
Grown from pieces of rhizome ("seed ginger") planted just under the soil surface; harvested by digging up the whole rhizome clump 8-10 months later, after the leaves yellow and die back.
Dried over open flame, giving it a smoky character distinct from green cardamom despite the shared name.
Often called the third most expensive spice by weight, after saffron and vanilla.
Native to the Western Ghats of southern India.
Turmeric's vivid yellow pigment, curcumin, has been used for thousands of years across South Asia not just as a spice but as a dye and a ceremonial and religious pigment.
Like its relative ginger, turmeric's flavorful part is an underground rhizome, not a true root.
Grown from rhizome pieces like ginger; the rhizomes are boiled, sun-dried, and polished after harvest, then ground into the bright yellow powder sold as a spice.
Though it resembles ginger, galangal has a sharper, more citrusy and piney bite, and is a staple aromatic in Thai and Indonesian dishes like tom kha gai.
Propagated from rhizome divisions; mature rhizomes are dug up after a year or more, when the tough, fibrous flesh is at its most pungent, and used fresh or dried and ground.

families.name: Musaceae
families.trait: Giant herbaceous plants with a false trunk (pseudostem) built from tightly rolled leaf sheaths, topped by huge paddle-shaped leaves and a hanging flower spike that develops into a cluster of fruit.
families.differentia: The order's giant, unmistakably fruit-bearing herb — its rolled-leaf pseudostem trunk has nothing in common with the low aromatic rhizomes of Zingiberaceae.

funFacts.text: Commercial bananas like the Cavendish are seedless, sterile triploids propagated only from cuttings, making every plant a genetic clone of the last — which leaves the entire global crop uniformly vulnerable to diseases like Panama disease.

Propagated from suckers growing at the base of a mature plant rather than seed, since cultivated bananas are seedless; the whole flowering stalk is cut down once the fruit fills out but is still green, and it ripens off the plant.

children.desc: Large-leaved tropical herbs with asymmetric, showy flowers and aromatic rhizomes or fruit-bearing pseudostems, source of most of the world's culinary spices from tropical Asia.

children.name: Arecales
children.quizClue: Several lines fanning out symmetrically from the top of a trunk.
children.quizWhy: This order is the palms, whose leaves (fronds) fan out symmetrically from the crown of an unbranched trunk.

families.name: Arecaceae
families.trait: Unbranched trunk crowned by a rosette of large fan- or feather-shaped fronds; flowers cluster on a branched inflorescence emerging from among the leaf bases.
families.differentia: The order's sole family and one of the most recognizable growth forms in the plant kingdom — an unbranched trunk topped by a permanent crown of fronds, found nowhere else among Poales' commelinid relatives.

funFacts.text: Botanically a drupe, not a true nut.
Its buoyant, waterproof husk lets coconuts float and stay viable for weeks at sea, which helped the species colonize remote tropical shorelines by ocean current long before humans carried it.

Grown from whole seed nuts germinated in a nursery bed before transplanting; mature nuts are harvested by climbing the trunk or using a long pole knife, then husked, and the flesh is pressed or dried into copra for oil.
Date palms grow as separate male and female trees, and only the females bear fruit — growers have hand-pollinated female flowers for thousands of years to guarantee a harvest.
A roughly 2,000-year-old date palm seed recovered at Masada, Israel, was germinated in 2005 and grew into a tree now nicknamed "Methuselah."

Female trees are hand-pollinated with pollen from male trees, since wind pollination alone is unreliable in cultivation; the fruit clusters are harvested over weeks as individual dates ripen, then sun-dried or dehydrated.

children.desc: The palms — unbranched, long-lived trees and shrubs topped by a permanent crown of large fronds, dominant across tropical and subtropical landscapes worldwide.

children.name: Ranunculales
children.quizClue: A simple flower made of eight thin lines radiating from a center dot.
children.quizWhy: Buttercups and poppies are classic examples of this early-diverging eudicot order, often with simple, radially symmetric flowers.

families.name: Ranunculaceae
families.trait: Simple, often deeply lobed leaves and radially symmetric flowers with numerous separate stamens and pistils spiraling around a raised center; many contain acrid, mildly toxic compounds.
families.differentia: The order's namesake family — flowers built from many separate, spirally arranged stamens and pistils rather than the fused, latex-bearing capsule fruit of Papaveraceae.

funFacts.text: Contains ranunculin, which breaks down into an irritant that can blister skin and mouths — grazing animals generally avoid it, and it can taint milk when eaten by dairy cattle.

families.name: Papaveraceae
families.trait: Milky or colored latex sap in stems and leaves; four delicate, crumpled petals opening from a nodding bud, with seeds housed in a capsule that shakes them out through pores.
families.differentia: Distinguished from Ranunculaceae's many-parted spiral flowers by milky latex sap and a four-petaled bloom that opens from a distinctively crumpled, nodding bud.

funFacts.text: The flower of Remembrance Day and Armistice Day poppies, inspired by the World War I poem "In Flanders Fields," where they grew abundantly on disturbed battlefield soil.
A different species from the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) — the common poppy contains only trace, non-narcotic alkaloids and isn't a source of opium.

children.desc: Herbaceous plants near the base of the eudicot family tree, retaining relatively primitive flowers with numerous separate floral parts rather than the fused structures common in later-diverging orders.

children.name: Proteales
children.quizClue: A spiky burst of lines around a solid center circle.
children.quizWhy: This order is a botanical grab-bag — sycamores, lotus, and the spiky-flowered Proteaceae — united by DNA more than by shared looks.

families.name: Platanaceae
families.trait: Mottled, flaking bark that peels away in patches; ball-shaped clusters of tiny fruits (achenes) dangling on long stalks; large, palmately lobed leaves.
families.differentia: Unlike the aquatic Nelumbonaceae or nut-bearing Proteaceae, this family is built around mottled, exfoliating bark and ball-shaped fruit clusters dangling from waterside trees.

funFacts.text: A hybrid between an American and an Oriental plane species, first arising in 17th-century Europe and now one of the most widely planted street trees in cities worldwide for its pollution tolerance.

families.name: Nelumbonaceae
families.trait: Aquatic perennials with rounded, waxy leaves and flower stalks held well above the water; unlike true water lilies, both leaf and flower rise clear of the surface on separate stalks.
families.differentia: The order's only aquatic family — both leaf and flower rise on separate stalks well above the water, unlike the streamside trees of Platanaceae or the woody shrubs of Proteaceae.

funFacts.text: In the early 1990s, UCLA scientist Jane Shen-Miller led a team that recovered and radiocarbon-dated a lotus seed from a dry lakebed in Liaoning Province, China, at roughly 1,300 years old — still viable, germinating within days. Japanese botanist Ichiro Ohga had made similar centuries-old finds at the same site decades earlier.
Its leaves and seed pods stay dry through a self-cleaning surface texture, later named the "lotus effect" and used as a model for water-repellent industrial coatings.
A central symbol in Buddhism and Hinduism, representing purity rising untouched from muddy water.

families.name: Proteaceae
families.trait: Flowers packed into dense, often brush- or cone-like inflorescences with narrow, radiating floral parts; woody, nut- or cone-like fruiting structures typical of nutrient-poor soils.
families.differentia: The order's namesake family — distinguished from Platanaceae's bark and Nelumbonaceae's water-lily-like habit by dense, brush-like flower clusters and woody, nut-bearing fruit.

funFacts.text: Native to the rainforests of northeastern Australia, though most commercial production today happens in Hawaii.
Toxic to dogs even in small amounts, causing weakness, vomiting, and tremors — one of relatively few common nuts that pose a real hazard to pets.

children.desc: A small but ancient order spanning three unrelated-looking families — sycamores, lotuses, and the showy Proteaceae — grouped together by DNA rather than any shared appearance, an early-diverging lineage near the base of the eudicots.

children.name: Vitales
children.quizClue: A cluster of small overlapping circles hanging together like a bunch.
children.quizWhy: Grapes are the signature plant of this order, growing in dense hanging clusters.

families.name: Vitaceae
families.trait: Woody, climbing vines that grip supports with coiling tendrils opposite the leaves; fruit forms in dense hanging clusters of juicy berries.
families.differentia: The order's sole family — tendril-climbing vines and clustered berry fruit define a growth habit found nowhere else this close to the base of the rosid clade.

funFacts.text: One of the oldest domesticated fruit crops, with winemaking evidence dating back roughly 8,000 years in the region of modern Georgia.
In the late 1800s, European vineyards were nearly wiped out by phylloxera, an aphid-like insect, and were saved largely by grafting European vines onto resistant American rootstock.

Vines are pruned hard every winter back to just a few buds, which controls yield and concentrates flavor; grapes destined for wine are picked once sugar levels peak, then crushed and left to ferment with their own skins.

children.desc: A single-family order of climbing woody vines, an early-diverging lineage near the base of the rosid clade.

children.name: Saxifragales
children.quizClue: Four thin ribbon-like strips arranged in a plus-sign around a center dot, instead of rounded petals.
children.quizWhy: Witch hazel (Hamamelidaceae) has unusually thin, strap-shaped petals instead of the rounded petals typical of most flowers.

families.name: Paeoniaceae
families.trait: Large, often ruffled flowers with numerous overlapping petals surrounding a prominent central boss of stamens; herbaceous or woody perennials that die back to a rootstock or persist as a shrub.
families.differentia: The order's showiest bloomer — its large ruffled flower has nothing in common with Hamamelidaceae's thin ribbon petals, Grossulariaceae's berry racemes, or Altingiaceae's spiky seed balls.

funFacts.text: Known historically as the "king of flowers" in China, especially prized in the city of Luoyang during the Tang dynasty.
Its root has a long history of use in traditional Chinese medicine.

families.name: Hamamelidaceae
families.trait: Small ribbon-like petals, often four per flower, opening directly on bare twigs in late fall or winter when little else blooms; witch hazel extract is distilled from its bark and leaves.
families.differentia: Distinguished from its Saxifragales relatives by unusually thin, strap-shaped petals opening in small clusters directly on leafless winter twigs.

funFacts.text: One of very few temperate trees that flower in late fall or even winter, after most other plants have gone dormant.
Its bark and leaf extract is distilled into a mild astringent widely used in skincare, a use with roots in Indigenous North American medicine.

families.name: Grossulariaceae
families.trait: Small, thornless-to-spiny shrubs bearing translucent berries strung in loose hanging racemes rather than one dense cluster.
families.differentia: Unlike Vitales' tightly packed grape bunches, this family's berries hang individually spaced along a thin raceme.

funFacts.text: In the early 1900s, plant pathologists identified Ribes species as the alternate host required by white pine blister rust to complete its life cycle, leading the U.S. to ban currant and gooseberry cultivation nationwide from 1911 to 1966 to protect the timber industry — black currant bore the brunt of the restrictions, though red currant was affected in some states too.

families.name: Altingiaceae
families.trait: Star-shaped, palmately lobed leaves that color brilliantly in autumn; round, spiky woody seed capsules ("gumballs") hang from long stalks.
families.differentia: The order's only family with a spiky, ball-shaped woody fruit — unlike the ribbon petals of Hamamelidaceae, the ruffled blooms of Paeoniaceae, or the currant racemes of Grossulariaceae.

funFacts.text: Named for the aromatic resin (storax) beneath its bark; Indigenous peoples of the southeastern United States chewed the hardened resin as an early natural chewing gum, a practice later adopted by European settlers.
Produces spiky, ball-shaped seed pods that persist on the tree through winter and are a familiar lawn nuisance in much of the southeastern U.S.

children.desc: A structurally diverse order of shrubs, perennials, and trees with little in common visually — from ruffled peony blooms to spiky sweetgum seed balls — grouped together primarily by shared ancestry near the base of the rosid clade.

funFacts.text: The name refers to a shared evolutionary predisposition, not a universal trait. All four orders here (Fabales, Fagales, Cucurbitales, Rosales) descend from one ancestor that gained the genetic toolkit for root-nodule symbiosis with nitrogen-fixing bacteria, but the trait itself is patchy across their descendants — expressed by most legumes and by alder (Fagales), yet absent from close relatives like hazelnut, which sits in the very same family as nitrogen-fixing alder.

children.name: Fagales
children.quizClue: Two mirrored curling lobes that together suggest a leaf, or an acorn cap.
children.quizWhy: Oaks, beeches, and chestnuts are classic members of this order, known for lobed leaves and nuts held in a cupule or husk.
children.desc: Wind-pollinated trees and shrubs of temperate and montane forests, bearing catkins and one-seeded nuts often cradled in a cupule, husk, or spiny bur.

families.name: Fagaceae
families.trait: Nuts (acorns, beechnuts, chestnuts) seated in a scaly or spiny cupule; lobed or toothed simple leaves.
families.differentia: The only family here with nuts seated in a true cupule (acorn cap, beech husk, chestnut bur) — Betulaceae and Juglandaceae both drop that structure for catkin-borne nutlets or fleshy husks instead.

funFacts.text: A single mature oak can produce tens of thousands of acorns in a good "mast year," a boom-and-bust cycle that helps overwhelm acorn-eating animals so enough seeds survive to sprout.
Long a national symbol across much of Europe, historically prized for shipbuilding timber strong enough to frame naval fleets.
The only tree whose bark is harvested commercially as cork — the thick outer bark is stripped by hand roughly every 9 to 12 years without harming the tree, which regrows it each time.
Portugal produces roughly half of the world's cork, from managed cork oak forests called montados.
Its smooth gray bark famously never develops the deep furrows of most mature trees, which is why beech trunks are a favorite surface for carved initials.
Roasted chestnuts have been a staple winter food across Europe for centuries, and chestnut flour was historically a bread substitute in mountainous regions where wheat grew poorly.

families.name: Betulaceae
families.trait: Papery, often peeling bark; separate male and female catkins on the same tree, small winged nutlets.
families.differentia: Shares catkins with Fagaceae but skips the cupule entirely; known instead for thin, often peeling bark and small winged nutlets.

funFacts.text: Its thin, papery white bark peels naturally in horizontal strips and was historically used by various cultures as a writing surface and for canoe-building.
The hazelnut of commerce, central to products like Nutella and widely grown in Turkey, which produces the large majority of the world's supply.
Like legumes, it hosts nitrogen-fixing bacteria in its roots (Frankia, not Rhizobium), letting it thrive in the wet, nutrient-poor soils along riverbanks where it commonly grows.
Its extremely dense, hard wood earned it the nickname "ironwood" in some regions, and it was historically used for tool handles and cogs in early wooden machinery.

families.name: Juglandaceae
families.trait: Pinnately compound aromatic leaves; drupe-like nuts encased in a fleshy husk over a hard shell.
families.differentia: Sets itself apart with aromatic pinnately compound leaves and a fleshy husk over a hard-shelled nut, unlike the cupule- or catkin-only fruiting of its relatives.

funFacts.text: Despite the common name "English walnut," it's native to Central Asia and the Middle East — English merchants simply popularized its trade across Europe.

Produces juglone, a chemical released from its roots and fallen leaves that suppresses the growth of many nearby plants, including tomatoes — a well-known hazard for gardeners planting near black walnut trees.
Native to North America and the official state tree or nut of several U.S. states, including Texas.
Its name comes from an Algonquian word referring to nuts requiring a stone to crack.
Named for its shaggy, loosely peeling bark plates, a distinctive identifying feature among North American hardwoods.
Its wood is a favorite for smoking meat, prized for the strong, sweet smoke flavor it imparts.

families.name: Myricaceae
families.trait: Resin-dotted, fragrant leaves; small waxy drupes historically boiled for candle tallow.
families.differentia: The order's outlier: small, resin-dotted shrubs with waxy drupes rather than the nuts that define the three larger Fagales families.

funFacts.text: Its waxy berry coating was boiled down by early American colonists to make bayberry candles, historically valued for burning cleaner and less smoky than tallow.
Used since medieval times as a bittering and flavoring agent in "gale beer," a traditional ale style that predates the widespread use of hops.
Almost entirely wind-pollinated, producing the dangling catkins that give oaks, birches, and walnuts their characteristic spring flowers.

children.name: Fabales
children.quizClue: A tall narrow capsule divided into four horizontal sections, like peas visible inside a pod.
children.quizWhy: Beans, peas, and lentils are legumes — their seeds develop in sections inside a single elongated pod.

families.name: Fabaceae
families.trait: Compound leaves and pea-like flowers with five petals arranged into a banner, wings, and keel; seeds develop inside a single elongated pod that splits along two seams; many host nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules.
families.differentia: The order's sole family and one of the plant kingdom's most important nitrogen-fixers — a trait rare outside this family.

funFacts.text: Sends taproots several meters deep, letting it draw on groundwater and survive drought far better than most forage crops.
A perennial hay crop cut several times a season, just as flowering begins for peak protein content, then field-dried or dried faster with a mechanical conditioner before baling.
The bean most commonly sprouted for the crunchy "bean sprouts" used across Asian cuisine.

Source of natural indigo dye, used for millennia across Asia, Africa, and the Americas — including the original blue dye for denim jeans, before synthetic indigo largely replaced it in the early 20th century.
One of the earliest crops domesticated in the Fertile Crescent, alongside wheat and barley, roughly 10,000 years ago.

Direct-seeded like other pulses; the whole plant is cut or pulled once the pods dry and rattle, then threshed to separate the small lens-shaped seeds, which are stored dry rather than processed further.
An extremely long-lived woody vine — Japan's famous century-old specimens can spread across enormous trellises supported by steel frameworks.
Domesticated independently in both Mesoamerica and the Andes, producing two genetically distinct lineages that were later crossed by breeders.
Ground into a naturally sweet powder often used as a caffeine-free chocolate substitute.
Nicknamed "St. John's bread" from a tradition holding that its pods sustained John the Baptist in the wilderness.
Produces exceptionally hard, rot-resistant wood historically used for fence posts, ship pegs, and railway ties.

Gregor Mendel's pea-breeding experiments in an Austrian monastery garden during the 1850s–60s, tracking traits like seed shape and flower color across generations, established the basic laws of inheritance and founded the modern science of genetics.

Nicknamed the "sensitive plant" for its leaves, which rapidly fold shut within seconds of being touched — a defensive reflex called thigmonasty, rare among plants for happening fast enough to watch in real time.
Its common name comes from a legend that Judas Iscariot hanged himself from a tree of this species.
Its pink flowers sprout directly from old bark and even the trunk itself, not just young twigs — a growth habit called cauliflory.
Its feathery leaflets fold up at night and during rain, a movement called nyctinasty — the same trick used by its more famous relative, the sensitive plant (Mimosa pudica).
Native to a broad swath of Asia from Iran to Japan, it is now widely planted as an ornamental shade tree well beyond its native range.
Partners with Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules, trading sugars for fixed nitrogen — one of the clearest, best-studied examples of the symbiosis that gives the Nitrogen-fixing clade its name.
Often sown as a living "green manure" alongside pasture grasses, since the nitrogen it fixes enriches the soil for neighboring plants without any synthetic fertilizer.
Usually sown directly into pasture or as a cover crop rather than harvested for its own sake; when grown for seed, the flower heads are cut and dried, then threshed to release the tiny seeds.

Grown in rotation with cereal crops in many farming systems, since their root-nodule bacteria replenish soil nitrogen that heavy grain cropping depletes - a practice far older than the chemistry that later explained why it worked.

children.desc: The order's sole family, and one of the plant kingdom's most important nitrogen-fixers — nearly every member here partners with root-nodule bacteria to convert atmospheric nitrogen into usable nutrients.

funFacts.text: Most legumes host nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules, converting atmospheric nitrogen into a form plants can use — a partnership that makes this family one of the most important in agriculture for building soil fertility.

children.name: Rosales
children.quizClue: Five overlapping circles arranged in a ring, forming a simple rounded bloom.
children.quizWhy: Roses, apples, and cherries belong to this order, many sharing the layered, overlapping-petal look of the rose family.

families.name: Rosaceae
families.trait: Five-petaled flowers arranged around a central disc of many stamens; an astonishing range of fruit types across the family — fleshy pomes (apple, pear), stone fruits (cherry, peach, apricot, almond), and aggregate fruits (strawberry, rose hips).
families.differentia: The order's largest and namesake family — its five-petaled, many-stamened flower is the shared thread beneath a remarkable range of fruit types, unlike the single-seeded fruits of Moraceae, Ulmaceae, and Cannabaceae.

funFacts.text: Cultivated for over 5,000 years, with this species historically central to the perfume and rosewater industry of Provins, France.
Its seed kernels contain amygdalin, which breaks down into cyanide compounds — eating more than a few raw kernels can cause poisoning.
The wild ancestor of most cultivated sweet cherry varieties grown today.
Originated in China, despite its scientific name — Europeans encountered it via Persia along Silk Road trade routes and assumed that was its homeland.
One of the longest-cultivated fruit trees, with thousands of named varieties bred over centuries.
Doesn't grow true from seed — a seed from a Honeycrisp apple won't produce another Honeycrisp tree, which is why every commercial apple tree is a grafted clone of the original variety.
Traces back to wild forests of Malus sieversii in the mountains of Kazakhstan, the species' original center of diversity.
