Nearly all cultivated varieties are grafted onto rootstock rather than grown from seed, since seedlings don't reliably reproduce the parent's fruit; grafted trees are pruned each winter to an open shape and hand-picked at harvest to avoid bruising.
Not a true botanical berry — the red fleshy part is swollen receptacle tissue, and the actual fruits are the tiny dot-like achenes on its surface, each containing one seed.

A close relative of peach and cherry in the same genus; wild almonds are bitter and contain the same cyanide-releasing compound as apricot kernels, but a single gene mutation, selected by early farmers, produced the sweet almonds grown today.
Trees are shaken mechanically once the outer hull splits open, dropping the in-shell nuts to the orchard floor, where they're swept up, hulled, and dried before the shell is cracked.
Most cultivated tree fruits in this family are grafted onto a separate rootstock rather than grown from seed, which keeps the variety true and lets growers control the tree's ultimate size.

families.name: Moraceae
families.trait: Milky latex sap throughout; flowers reduced and often clustered inside a fleshy receptacle (as in figs) or along drooping catkins (as in mulberry).
families.differentia: Distinguished by milky latex sap and flowers hidden inside a fleshy structure or catkin, unlike the showy, five-petaled blooms of Rosaceae.

funFacts.text: Many fig species rely on tiny, species-specific fig wasps for pollination, one of the most tightly evolved plant-insect mutualisms known — though most commercially grown fig varieties are seedless and don't require it.
The near-exclusive food source of silkworm (Bombyx mori) larvae, making it central to the multi-thousand-year history of silk production in China.
Its dark, juicy berries are sweeter and more tart than white mulberry, though it is the white mulberry leaf, not black, that silkworms are traditionally raised on.

families.name: Urticaceae
families.trait: Leaves and stems covered in stinging hairs (trichomes) that inject irritant compounds on contact; small, inconspicuous wind-pollinated flowers.
families.differentia: The order's only family defined by defensive stinging hairs, unlike the latex of Moraceae or the fibrous stems of Cannabaceae and Ulmaceae.

funFacts.text: Its hollow hairs act like microscopic hypodermic needles, injecting histamine and other irritants on contact — but young leaves become harmless and edible once cooked or dried, which neutralizes the sting.

families.name: Cannabaceae
families.trait: Palmately compound leaves with narrow, serrated leaflets radiating from a central point; separate male and female plants, flowers reduced and wind- or insect-pollinated.
families.differentia: Immediately recognizable by its palmate, multi-fingered leaf — a leaf shape shared by no other family in this order.

funFacts.text: Industrial hemp and psychoactive cannabis are the same species — they differ mainly in THC content as a result of selective breeding, which is why many countries set a legal THC threshold to distinguish the two uses.

Grown densely for fiber (tall, minimally branched stalks cut and retted like flax) or spaced further apart for seed and flower; fiber and seed varieties are harvested at entirely different maturity stages.

families.name: Ulmaceae
families.trait: Asymmetric leaf bases (one side larger than the other) with doubly toothed margins; small, round, papery-winged seeds (samaras) that disperse on the wind.
families.differentia: Set apart by lopsided, asymmetric leaf bases and small round winged seeds, distinct from the compound leaves and fleshy fruit of its Rosales relatives.

funFacts.text: American elm populations were devastated across the 20th century by Dutch elm disease, a fungus spread by bark beetles and named for the Dutch scientists who first identified it, not for its origin.

children.desc: A remarkably diverse order uniting the classic five-petaled rose-family fruits with the latex-bearing figs, stinging nettles, fibrous hemp, and wind-pollinated elms — five families with little in common beyond shared ancestry.

children.name: Cucurbitales
children.quizClue: A round ridged fruit with a small stem nub on top, like a tiny melon or pumpkin.
children.quizWhy: Squash and melons belong to this order, producing large fleshy fruits that are often ridged along their length.

families.name: Cucurbitaceae
families.trait: Sprawling or climbing vines that grip supports with coiling tendrils; large, often ridged fruits with a thick rind (pepo) enclosing numerous flat seeds.
families.differentia: The order's defining family — tendril-climbing vines and large ridged pepo fruits are found nowhere else this close to the Fabids clade.

funFacts.text: One of the "Three Sisters" traditionally companion-planted with corn and beans by Indigenous peoples of North America, each crop supporting the others.
An extremely genetically diverse species — cantaloupe, honeydew, and many other melon types once thought to be separate species are all variants of Cucumis melo.
Botanically a fruit, not a vegetable — it develops from a pollinated flower and carries seeds, even though it's almost always eaten and prepared like a vegetable.
Cucumbers are roughly 95% water by weight, among the highest water content of any commonly eaten produce.

children.desc: The order's defining family — tendril-climbing vines and large ridged fruits found nowhere else this close to the Fabids clade.

children.name: Malpighiales
children.quizClue: Five short rounded petals around a center dot — a plain, flat little flower.
children.quizWhy: This is one of the largest and most diverse rosid orders — flax, violets, and cassava all sit here despite looking quite different.

families.name: Linaceae
families.trait: Slender, wiry stems yielding strong bast fibers (the source of linen); small, delicate five-petaled flowers, often blue.
families.differentia: The order's fiber specialist — wiry stems and delicate blue flowers set it apart from the latex, stinging hairs, or elaborate blooms of its Malpighiales relatives here.

funFacts.text: In 2009, paleobiologist Eliso Kvavadze found spun, dyed flax fibers while examining pollen samples from Dzudzuana Cave in Georgia — radiocarbon dating placed them at roughly 30,000 years old, the oldest known evidence of humans processing plant fiber into cordage or cloth.
The same crop yields two very different products depending on how it's grown: linseed oil from the seeds, and linen fiber from the stem.

For fiber, whole plants are pulled up rather than cut, then "retted" - soaked or left in damp conditions for weeks so bacteria break down the stem's pectin, freeing the long bast fibers for spinning into linen.

families.name: Salicaceae
families.trait: Separate male and female plants bearing soft, fuzzy catkins in early spring, often before leaves emerge; fast-growing trees and shrubs of moist habitats.
families.differentia: The order's only family with soft, fuzzy spring catkins, unlike the fibrous stems of Linaceae or the showy blooms of Violaceae and Passifloraceae.

funFacts.text: Its fuzzy, soft catkins are actually clusters of small flowers, not fruit or seed structures.
Willow bark contains salicin, the natural compound that inspired the development of aspirin in the 19th century.
Its bark contains salicin, a compound chemically related to aspirin, and has been chewed or brewed for pain and fever relief since antiquity — a direct ancestor of the modern painkiller.

families.name: Violaceae
families.icon: <circle cx="20" cy="20" r="2"/><ellipse cx="20" cy="12" rx="5" ry="6"/><ellipse cx="12" cy="20" rx="6" ry="5"/><ellipse cx="28" cy="20" rx="6" ry="5"/><ellipse cx="20" cy="28" rx="7" ry="6"/><path d="M20 28v5"/>
families.trait: Five-petaled flowers with a distinct, enlarged lower petal often extended into a nectar spur, giving many species an asymmetric, face-like bloom.
families.differentia: Distinguished by an asymmetric, face-like flower with one enlarged spurred petal, unlike the radially symmetric blooms elsewhere in this order.

funFacts.text: Its scent compound, ionone, briefly desensitizes the human nose's smell receptors, which is why the fragrance seems to fade after a few seconds and then reappear.
Its flowers have long been candied and used to decorate desserts and confections.

families.name: Hypericaceae
families.trait: Yellow flowers with numerous long, thread-like stamens forming a prominent central tuft; leaves often dotted with translucent oil glands.
families.differentia: Set apart by a dense starburst of long stamens tipped with visible anthers, denser than the simple radiating flowers found elsewhere in the order.

funFacts.text: Named for its tendency to bloom around the feast of St. John the Baptist, June 24th.
Widely used as an herbal remedy for mild depression, though it can dangerously reduce the effectiveness of many prescription medications by speeding up how the liver breaks them down.

families.name: Passifloraceae
families.trait: Elaborate flowers with a fringed corona of thread-like filaments encircling the reproductive parts; climbing vines with tendrils, producing a many-seeded pulpy fruit.
families.differentia: Unmistakable for its fringed corona of filaments ringing the flower center, a structure unique to this family in the order.

funFacts.text: Named by Spanish missionaries who saw the flower's intricate structure — its corona, tendrils, and other parts — as symbols of Christ's Passion, not romantic passion.

families.name: Euphorbiaceae
families.trait: Milky, often caustic latex sap throughout; tiny flowers lacking petals, clustered into a cup-shaped structure (cyathium) that mimics a single flower.
families.differentia: The order's only family built around a caustic milky latex and a flower-mimicking cyathium cup, spanning everything from tiny weeds to the starchy cassava root.

funFacts.text: Known in Australia as "radium weed" for its traditional bush-medicine use treating skin lesions; a compound extracted from its milky, irritant sap is now the active ingredient in a prescription treatment for a type of precancerous skin condition.

Contains cyanogenic compounds that must be removed by soaking, fermenting, or cooking before eating, especially in "bitter" varieties — despite this, it's a dietary staple for several hundred million people across the tropics.

Grown from stem cuttings planted directly in the ground; the starchy roots are dug up 8-24 months later and must be peeled, grated, and pressed or soaked to leach out cyanogenic compounds before the pulp is dried into flour.

families.name: Malpighiaceae
families.trait: Twining woody vines and shrubs with opposite, often glossy leaves; five clawed, fringed petals surround a pair of oil-secreting glands on the sepals that attract specialized bees across their mostly New World range.
families.differentia: The order's vine specialist — unlike the fibrous Linaceae, catkin-bearing Salicaceae, spurred Violaceae blooms, starburst-stamened Hypericaceae, corona-fringed Passifloraceae, or latex-oozing Euphorbiaceae, this family is built around twining lianas with clawed, fringed petals and paired oil glands.

funFacts.text: Most Malpighiaceae flowers secrete oil instead of nectar, from paired glands on the sepals, to attract a small group of specialized oil-collecting bees found mainly in the Americas.
Central to shamanic ceremonies across the Amazon basin for centuries, the vine is typically brewed together with other plants into a ritual beverage that shares the name ayahuasca.
The vine itself isn't psychoactive on its own — it works by inhibiting enzymes that would otherwise break down the DMT supplied by the other plant brewed alongside it.

children.desc: One of the largest and most heterogeneous rosid orders, uniting fiber crops, willows, violets, passionflowers, and spurges with little visual common ground — a grouping defined almost entirely by DNA rather than shared form.

children.name: Oxalidales
children.quizClue: Three overlapping circles arranged like a three-part clover leaf.
children.quizWhy: Wood sorrel (Oxalis) is famous for its three-part, clover-like leaves, which fold up at night.

families.name: Oxalidaceae
families.trait: Compound leaves typically divided into three heart-shaped leaflets that fold downward at night or in low light (nyctinasty); sour, oxalic-acid-rich tissue gives the family its name.
families.differentia: The order's defining family — its three-part, light-sensitive clover-like leaves are a distinctive trait not shared by the order's other, more obscure families.

funFacts.text: Its clover-like leaflets fold downward at night or in bright sun, a light-sensitive movement called nyctinasty.
The leaves taste sharply sour from oxalic acid, earning it old English folk nicknames like "sourgrass" and "cuckoo bread," the latter tied to its bloom coinciding with the cuckoo's spring arrival.
Leaves fold shut at night or under bright midday sun, a light- and touch-sensitive movement called nyctinasty, most familiar in clover-like wood sorrel.
Wood sorrel's tangy, lemony leaves come from oxalic acid — the same compound, at much higher concentration, found in rhubarb leaves.

children.desc: Mostly herbaceous plants with light-sensitive, clover-like compound leaves and a sharp, oxalic-acid tang.

children.name: Geraniales
children.quizClue: Five uneven lines radiating from a center dot, an asymmetric little flower.
children.quizWhy: Geraniums have asymmetric five-petaled flowers with visible dark veining, unlike the more uniform flowers of related orders.

families.name: Geraniaceae
families.trait: Palmately lobed or deeply dissected leaves; flowers with five separate petals, often with fine dark veining, followed by a distinctive long, beak-shaped seed capsule that springs open to fling seeds away from the parent plant.
families.differentia: The order's defining family — its beaked seed capsule (the source of the common name "cranesbill") is unique among the Diagram's rosid orders.

funFacts.text: The common garden "geranium" sold at nurseries is technically a Pelargonium, a separate genus that 18th-century botanists split off from the true Geranium genus.
Most garden Pelargonium hybrids descend from wild species native to South Africa.
Named for its distinctive beaked seed capsule — the shape reminded early botanists of a crane's bill, from the Greek geranos, "crane."
As the seed capsule dries, it splits explosively from the base upward, catapulting seeds several meters from the parent plant.

children.desc: Herbs and shrubs with lobed leaves and five-petaled flowers, known for a distinctive beaked seed capsule that catapults seeds away from the parent plant.

children.name: Myrtales
children.quizClue: A cluster of fine hair-like lines fanning out from a small circle — more like stamens than petals.
children.quizWhy: Eucalyptus and myrtle flowers often skip showy petals entirely, relying instead on a dense burst of long stamens for color.

families.name: Myrtaceae
families.trait: Aromatic, oil-gland-dotted evergreen leaves; flowers often lacking showy petals, instead displaying a dense burst of long colorful stamens.
families.differentia: The order's namesake and dominant family — aromatic oil-dotted leaves and a stamen-dominated flower distinguish it from Lythraceae's crown-like, many-seeded fruit.

funFacts.text: Named because its flavor resembles a blend of cinnamon, nutmeg, and clove all at once — not because it's a mixture of spices.
Native to the Caribbean and Central America, unlike most spices historically sourced from Asia.
Koalas feed almost exclusively on eucalyptus leaves, which are toxic or unpalatable to most other mammals due to the tree's strong essential oils.
Harvested as dried, unopened flower buds.
Native only to Indonesia's Maluku Islands, part of the same historic spice-trade rivalry that also centered on nutmeg from the neighboring Banda Islands.
The unopened flower buds are hand-picked while still green-pink and spread out to dry in the sun for several days, turning the familiar dark brown as they lose most of their moisture.

families.name: Lythraceae
families.trait: Tubular flowers with crinkled, crepe-like petals in many relatives; pomegranate itself bears a tough-skinned fruit crowned by a persistent calyx and packed with juicy seed arils.
families.differentia: The order's only family here with a crown-topped, many-seeded fruit, unlike the stamen-heavy flowers typical of Myrtaceae.

funFacts.text: A symbol of fertility and abundance across many Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cultures for thousands of years.
A single fruit can contain several hundred individual seed-and-pulp arils.
Fruit is snipped rather than pulled from the branch, since tugging can split the tough rind; it's harvested when it makes a metallic sound when tapped, a sign the arils inside are fully juiced up.

children.desc: Aromatic trees and shrubs producing some of the world's most prized spices and timbers, dominated by oil-rich Myrtaceae alongside the crown-fruited pomegranate family, Lythraceae.

children.name: Brassicales
children.quizClue: Four dots connected by lines forming a perfect cross shape.
children.quizWhy: Mustards, cabbages, and radishes are named for their four-petaled “cruciform” flowers, arranged in a perfect cross.

families.name: Brassicaceae
families.trait: Four petals arranged in a perfect cross (cruciform); pungent mustard-oil glucosinolates throughout the tissue, released as a defense when cells are damaged.
families.differentia: The order's namesake and dominant family — its four-petaled cruciform flower and mustard-oil chemistry set every cabbage relative apart from the single-species outliers Capparaceae, Moringaceae, Caricaceae, and Tropaeolaceae.

funFacts.text: Cabbage, kale, broccoli, cauliflower, and Brussels sprouts are all the same species — selective breeding for different plant parts (leaves, flower buds, stem buds) over centuries produced these dramatically different-looking vegetables.

Started as seedlings and transplanted into the field; heads are cut at the base once they feel dense and firm, and a second, smaller flush of small heads can sometimes be harvested from the same stump afterward.
Its sharp pungency comes from allyl isothiocyanate, released only when the root's cells are damaged — the same chemical family responsible for mustard and wasabi's heat.
Lends its name, by scent association rather than direct derivation, to mustard gas, the chemical warfare agent first used in World War I — the gas isn't made from the plant itself.
Its peppery bite comes from glucosinolates, the same defensive compounds responsible for pungency across the mustard family.
One of the fastest-maturing vegetable crops, with some varieties ready to harvest in as little as three to four weeks.
One of the fastest crops from sowing to harvest, direct-seeded and ready to pull in as little as three to four weeks; left in the ground too long, the root turns woody and pithy.
The original jack-o'-lantern in Ireland and Scotland — turnips and other root vegetables were carved and lit before pumpkins became the standard in America.
A natural hybrid between cabbage and turnip, thought to have first arisen in gardens where the two grew side by side.

families.name: Capparaceae
families.trait: Flower buds are harvested and pickled before opening; mature flowers show four petals and a dramatic burst of long, thread-like stamens.
families.differentia: Distinguished from Brassicaceae's four-petaled cross by a dramatic burst of long stamens on a flower bud that's harvested before it ever opens.

funFacts.text: The pickled buds sold as capers are unopened flower buds, harvested by hand before they bloom; if left to mature, the resulting fruit is sometimes pickled too, as "caper berries."

families.name: Moringaceae
families.trait: Fast-growing trees with finely divided, fern-like compound leaves and extremely long, slender seed pods nicknamed "drumsticks."
families.differentia: The order's most distinctively shaped member — fern-like compound leaves and pods stretching over a foot long, unlike anything else in Brassicales.

funFacts.text: Nicknamed the "miracle tree" for its unusually nutrient-dense leaves, rich in vitamin C, calcium, and protein for a leafy green.
Its crushed seeds contain proteins that act as a natural coagulant, used in some communities to help purify cloudy drinking water.

families.name: Caricaceae
families.trait: Fast-growing, mostly unbranched trees with large, deeply lobed palmate leaves and large fleshy fruit borne directly on the trunk.
families.differentia: A fast-growing, nearly unbranched tree bearing fruit directly on its trunk, unlike the low herbs that make up most of this order.

funFacts.text: Contains papain, a protein-digesting enzyme extracted commercially and used as a natural meat tenderizer.

Grown from seed and fruiting within a year; fruit is cut when the skin just starts to blush yellow, since papayas continue ripening off the tree, and the still-green latex-rich sap is tapped separately for the papain used in meat tenderizer.

families.name: Tropaeolaceae
families.trait: Round, shield-shaped leaves with the stem attached at the center (peltate); showy, funnel-shaped flowers trailing a long nectar spur behind the petals.
families.differentia: Set apart by round, center-stalked (peltate) leaves and a flower trailing a long nectar spur, a shape found nowhere else in the order.

funFacts.text: Entirely edible, including the peppery flowers and leaves, which taste similar to watercress.

children.desc: A pungent order defined by mustard-oil glucosinolate chemistry, spanning the vast cabbage family alongside a handful of single-species outlier families — capers, moringa, papaya, and nasturtiums — each retaining the order's characteristic bite in its own way.

children.name: Malvales
children.quizClue: Five large, fully overlapping circles around a center dot — bigger and fuller than a plain rose-like bloom.
children.quizWhy: Hibiscus, cotton, and mallow flowers are typically large, with broad, overlapping rounded petals.

families.name: Malvaceae
families.trait: Flowers with five petals and numerous stamens fused into a central staminal column; many species yield fiber, chocolate, or cola-nut caffeine from very differently used plant parts.
families.differentia: The order's vastly broadened namesake family (folding in the old cotton, linden, and cacao families) — united by stamens fused into a central column, unlike Bixaceae's simple exposed stamens.

funFacts.text: The fluffy fiber harvested for textiles grows directly on the plant's seeds, not from a stem or leaf.
Domesticated independently in both the Americas and the Old World, from different wild Gossypium species.
Bolls are picked once they burst open and the fiber has fully fluffed out, either by hand or mechanical picker; the harvested lint is then ginned to separate the fiber from the seed.
Its genus name means "food of the gods" in Greek; the Aztec and Maya civilizations used cacao beans both as a ceremonial drink and as a form of currency.
Beans are fermented before being dried, roasted, and ground — a step essential for developing chocolate's characteristic flavor.

Pods are cut from the trunk and branches by hand, then split open so the pulp-covered beans can be scooped out and piled to ferment for several days - a step essential for developing chocolate flavor - before sun-drying and roasting.
Its flowers are steeped into a traditional herbal tea across Europe and are a major nectar source for honeybees, producing a distinctively flavored honey.
Releases a mucilage when cut and cooked that acts as a natural thickener, essential to dishes like Louisiana gumbo.

The large pale-yellow blossoms are edible too, with a mild flavor similar to the pod; they're eaten raw in salads, stuffed and fried like squash blossoms, or dipped in batter — but must be picked the single day they open, since each flower closes and wilts by the following morning.
Each individual flower typically lasts only a single day before wilting, even though the plant blooms continuously over a long season.
Its caffeine-containing seeds, kola nuts, were part of the original flavoring in early cola soft drink recipes, lending the drinks their name.
One of the most widely produced natural fibers after cotton, historically central to the economy of Bengal, and still a major source of burlap and sacking material.

Grown densely and cut near the base once the plant flowers; stalks are then retted in water for weeks to loosen the bark, which is stripped off by hand to separate the long fibers used for burlap and rope.
Its mucilage-rich leaves and flowers were used in ancient Greek and Roman medicine, and later across European folk traditions, to soothe sore throats and irritated skin.

families.name: Bixaceae
families.trait: Spiny, heart-shaped seed capsules split open to reveal small red-orange seeds coated in a natural dye (bixin) used for centuries as a coloring and spice.
families.differentia: The order's only family here defined by a spiny, dye-producing seed pod, unlike Malvaceae's fused-stamen flower.

funFacts.text: Its seed coating, bixin, has been used as a natural dye and body paint by Indigenous peoples of the Americas for centuries, and is still widely used today to color cheeses like cheddar and Red Leicester.

children.desc: A fiber-and-chocolate order dominated by a greatly broadened Malvaceae (absorbing the old cotton, linden, and cacao families), united by stamens fused into a distinctive central column.

children.name: Sapindales
children.quizClue: A single winged seed shape split by a line down the middle, like a maple seed spinning to the ground.
children.quizWhy: Maple, mango, and citrus belong here; the winged maple samara is one of the order's most recognizable seed shapes.
children.desc: Woody, mostly compound-leaved trees bearing a nectar-producing floral disc; unified less by any single trait than by a cluster of resin canals, bitter terpenoids, and saponins scattered across its families.

families.name: Anacardiaceae
families.trait: Resin canals bearing irritant compounds (urushiol); drupe fruits, often with milky or resinous sap.
families.differentia: Unlike Rutaceae's oil glands or Burseraceae's clear resin, this family's sap contains irritant urushiols — the trait that separates mango and cashew from their more benign Sapindales cousins.

funFacts.text: Native to South Asia, where it's been cultivated for over 4,000 years and holds status as India's national fruit.
Its skin and sap contain urushiol-related compounds, and people sensitive to poison ivy can develop a similar skin reaction from handling unpeeled mango.
Its tart, fuzzy red drupe clusters are dried and ground into a lemony spice used across Middle Eastern cooking, or steeped in water for a tangy, cold "sumac-ade."
The cashew "nut" grows outside the fleshy cashew apple, and its shell contains a caustic, urushiol-like resin that must be carefully roasted off before the nut inside is safe to eat.
The shell naturally splits open as the nut matures — a trait that made it easy to hand-sort ripe from unripe nuts long before mechanized processing.
Produces urushiol, an oily compound that triggers an allergic skin reaction in most people; the same chemical family shows up at lower levels throughout this family, including in mango and cashew.
Named for its airy, wispy flower clusters, which persist after blooming and give the whole shrub a hazy, smoke-like appearance from a distance.

Many members produce urushiol or closely related irritant oils — the compound responsible for poison ivy's rash also occurs, in lower concentrations, in mango skin and raw cashew shells, which is why cashews are always sold roasted or steamed rather than raw in the shell.

families.name: Rutaceae
families.trait: Aromatic oil glands dotting the leaves; flower parts in 4s or 5s around a prominent nectary disc.
families.differentia: Distinguished from the other resin-bearing families here by aromatic oil glands (not resin canals) and a citrus-type fruit found nowhere else in the order.

funFacts.text: A hybrid between pomelo and mandarin, not a naturally occurring wild species.
Also a hybrid, descended from a cross between bitter orange and citron.
Unusual among citrus for having a sweet, edible peel paired with tart flesh — most kumquats are eaten whole, skin and all.
Its sap can cause a light-triggered skin reaction called phytophotodermatitis, producing blistering or discoloration where sap-covered skin is exposed to sunlight.

Its aromatic leaves are a foundational flavoring in South Indian and Sri Lankan cooking, typically fried in hot oil at the start of a dish to release their fragrance — despite the name, they're unrelated to curry powder.

Nearly all citrus fruits grown today trace back to just a handful of wild ancestor species — pomelo, mandarin, and citron — with most familiar citrus, including oranges, lemons, and grapefruits, being natural or cultivated hybrids among them.

families.name: Sapindaceae
families.trait: Saponins concentrated in fruit and seed; the maple lineage contributes winged, paired samaras.
families.differentia: The only family in this order built around saponins and winged samaras — a fruit and chemistry profile distinct from the resins of Anacardiaceae/Burseraceae and the bitters of Meliaceae/Simaroubaceae.

funFacts.text: The source of most maple syrup — sap is collected in late winter when freezing nights and thawing days create the pressure changes that make it flow, then boiled down at roughly 40 parts sap to 1 part syrup.
Its glossy brown seeds ("conkers") contain saponins that are mildly toxic to humans, unlike the unrelated true chestnut, which is safe to eat.
The seeds are used in conkers, a traditional British playground game where players take turns striking each other's seed, threaded on a string.
Native to southern China, where it's been cultivated for over 2,000 years.
A close relative of lychee, distinguished by its soft, hairy spines — its name comes from the Malay word for "hair."
Named for its showy sprays of yellow flowers, followed by papery, lantern-like seed pods that persist into fall.
Unlike sugar maple, Norway maple oozes milky-white sap from a broken leaf stalk — a quick field trick for telling the two lookalike species apart.
Native to Europe and western Asia, it has become a widespread and sometimes invasive street tree across North America.

families.name: Meliaceae
families.trait: Bitter limonoid compounds throughout bark and wood; prized timber, pinnately compound leaves.
families.differentia: Shares bitter terpenoids with Simaroubaceae, but Meliaceae's are limonoids concentrated in prized timber wood, not the quassinoids of bark seen in its bitter-tasting sibling.

funFacts.text: Historically prized as one of the world's premier furniture and shipbuilding timbers, which drove overharvesting severe enough that the species is now protected under international trade regulations (CITES).
Used across South Asian traditional medicine for millennia, and its seed oil, containing the compound azadirachtin, is now also formulated into commercial organic pesticides.
Its berries are toxic to humans and many animals if eaten in quantity, though birds can consume them without harm and help spread the seeds.
Despite the name, not a true cedar (which are conifers) — its fragrant, insect-repellent wood is prized for cigar boxes and humidors.
Its young reddish shoots are a prized spring vegetable in Chinese cuisine, stir-fried or scrambled with eggs for their pungent, oniony aroma.

families.name: Burseraceae
families.trait: Aromatic resins exuded from wounded bark, which peels in papery layers; resin canals run throughout.
families.differentia: Closest chemically to Anacardiaceae, but its resin is aromatic and historically prized (frankincense, myrrh) rather than irritant, and bark peels papery instead of staying intact.

funFacts.text: Its dried resin, tapped from cuts in the bark, was one of the most valuable trade goods of the ancient world and is named in the Bible as one of the gifts brought to the infant Jesus.
Its resin was used in ancient Egypt as an ingredient in embalming, alongside its long-standing role as incense and perfume across the ancient Near East.
Named for its swollen, water-storing trunk, an adaptation to the arid deserts of the southwestern U.S. and Mexico where it grows.
Its aromatic resin, copal, has been burned as ceremonial incense in Mesoamerica since long before European contact and remains widely used in Mexican traditional and religious practice today.

Frankincense and myrrh were carried for thousands of years along the ancient Incense Route from southern Arabia to the Mediterranean, making this family central to one of history's oldest long-distance luxury trades.

families.name: Simaroubaceae
families.trait: Intensely bitter quassinoids in bark and wood; historically the family's namesake medicinal bitters.
families.differentia: The order's bitterest family by far — quassinoids here are intense enough for medicinal bitters, well beyond the milder limonoids of Meliaceae.

funFacts.text: Native to China, but a highly aggressive invasive species elsewhere, spreading through root suckers and chemically suppressing nearby plant growth.

The preferred host plant of the invasive spotted lanternfly in the United States — the insect survives and reproduces better on tree of heaven than on any other tree, making its removal a key part of controlling the pest's spread.
Its intensely bitter wood extract has long been used in traditional medicine and remains a flavoring agent in some bitters and aperitifs.
Named alongside Quassia amara for its similarly intense bitterness, historically leading both to be used interchangeably as sources of "quassia" extract.
One of the most chemically and economically diverse rosid orders, spanning mangoes and cashews, citrus fruits, maples, mahogany, and the resins frankincense and myrrh.
Its fruit and nut trees (citrus, mango, cashew, pistachio) are overwhelmingly propagated by grafting a fruiting variety onto a hardier seedling rootstock, rather than grown from seed.
Marks one of the two major splits within the rosids, roughly 100 million years ago — the other branch, Vitales, split off earlier and today is just grapes.
Contains tens of thousands of species, from grapes and roses to legumes, cotton, and citrus — bound together by shared ancestry rather than any single visible trait.

children.name: Santalales
children.quizClue: A sprig with paired leaves and two small round berries, like a mistletoe branch.
children.quizWhy: Mistletoe, a partial parasite that grows on host trees, belongs to this order.

families.name: Santalaceae
families.trait: Many members are hemiparasitic, tapping into a host tree's roots or branches for water and minerals while still photosynthesizing themselves; includes both fragrant heartwood trees and parasitic shrubs.
families.differentia: The order's defining family, spanning fragrant sandalwood trees and parasitic mistletoe shrubs — unified by a parasitic or hemiparasitic lifestyle uncommon elsewhere in the Diagram. (Modern classification folds the older mistletoe family, Viscaceae, into Santalaceae.)

funFacts.text: A hemiparasitic tree — its roots tap into the roots of nearby host plants for water and nutrients even though it also photosynthesizes on its own.

Its fragrant heartwood has been prized for incense, carving, and perfume across South and Southeast Asia for thousands of years, and overharvesting has made wild sandalwood one of the most heavily regulated timbers in the world.
A hemiparasite that taps into a host tree's water and mineral supply through specialized roots called haustoria, while still photosynthesizing green leaves of its own.
The Christmas kissing tradition traces back to European folklore, including Norse mythology, where mistletoe was associated with love and reconciliation.
Its sticky berries are spread by birds, particularly mistle thrushes, which wipe the seed-laden pulp off their beaks onto tree branches after eating.

children.desc: A largely parasitic or hemiparasitic order that taps into the roots or branches of host plants for water and nutrients while still carrying out its own photosynthesis.

children.name: Caryophyllales
children.quizClue: A rounded vertical capsule shape with a couple of small marks near its base, like a squat cactus.
children.quizWhy: This order includes cacti and other succulents, along with beets, spinach, and amaranth — a chemically distinctive group more than a visually uniform one.

families.name: Cactaceae
families.trait: Thick, water-storing succulent stems (often leafless) covered in spine clusters derived from modified leaves; flowers large and showy despite the plant's otherwise armored appearance.
families.differentia: The order's most extreme water-storage specialist — succulent, spine-covered stems set it apart from the leafy, pigment-rich herbs that dominate the rest of Caryophyllales here.

funFacts.text: Nearly all cacti use CAM photosynthesis, opening their pores only at night to minimize water loss — a key adaptation to arid environments.

families.name: Amaranthaceae
families.trait: Small, often colorless flowers packed into dense spikes or clusters; many species store energy in swollen roots, thick leaves, or protein-rich seeds, and several produce the reddish betalain pigments distinctive to this order.
families.differentia: The order's largest and most agriculturally important family here — small flowers crowded into dense spikes distinguish it from Polygonaceae's papery-sheathed stems and Portulacaceae's fleshy trailing leaves.

funFacts.text: Contains oxalic acid, which binds calcium and iron in the gut and somewhat reduces how much of those minerals the body can absorb from it.
Coated in bitter-tasting saponins that deter insects and birds; the seeds are rinsed or soaked before cooking to remove them.
Domesticated in the Andes thousands of years ago and a staple food of the Inca Empire.
Its red pigment, betanin, passes through the digestive system largely intact in some people, occasionally turning urine or stool pink or red — a harmless condition called beeturia.
The same species as beet and sugar beet — chard has simply been selectively bred for its leaves and stalks rather than its root.
Grows rooted in salt marshes and tidal flats, tolerating salinity levels that would kill most land plants — its common name, glasswort, comes from historical use of its ash in early glassmaking.
A staple grain of the Aztec Empire, used in religious rituals as well as food — a role that led Spanish colonizers to suppress its cultivation after the conquest.

families.name: Polygonaceae
families.trait: Jointed stems wrapped at each node by a papery sheath (ocrea); often sour, oxalic-acid-rich leaves, and small flowers clustered in loose spikes.
families.differentia: Set apart from its Caryophyllales relatives by a papery stem-sheath (ocrea) at each leaf node and a characteristically sour, oxalic-acid tang in the leaves.

funFacts.text: Ground into flour for Japanese soba noodles and Breton galettes, valued partly because it's naturally gluten-free.
Its leaves contain high levels of oxalic acid and are toxic if eaten in quantity, while the stalks — the only part normally eaten — are safe.
Botanically a vegetable, though a 19th-century U.S. customs ruling classified it as a fruit for tariff purposes because of how it's eaten, a classification that stuck in everyday use.
Gets its sharp, tangy taste from oxalic acid, the same compound found in rhubarb leaves, though at far lower concentrations safe for normal culinary use.
Despite the name, buckwheat isn't a wheat or even a grass — it's a broadleaf plant in this family, only superficially resembling cereal grains in how its starchy seeds are used.

families.name: Portulacaceae
families.trait: Low, trailing succulent stems with small, fleshy paddle-shaped leaves; short-lived flowers open only in sunlight and close by afternoon.
families.differentia: The order's low, mat-forming succulent — fleshy paddle leaves on trailing stems distinguish it from the upright spikes of Amaranthaceae and the jointed, sheathed stems of Polygonaceae.

funFacts.text: One of the few leafy vegetables containing meaningful amounts of omega-3 fatty acids, unusual for a plant source.
Considered a nutritious vegetable in many cuisines but treated as a weed in others, sometimes growing in the same garden bed as a crop and a nuisance depending on who's asked.

children.desc: A chemically distinctive order spanning cacti, succulents, and leafy vegetables, many sharing unusual reddish betalain pigments (instead of the anthocyanins used elsewhere in flowering plants) as well as a tendency toward salt- and drought-tolerance.

funFacts.text: An unusually diverse order for its size, spanning cacti, carnivorous plants, and many of the world's leafy and root vegetables — grouped together by DNA rather than shared appearance.

children.name: Cornales
children.icon: <ellipse cx="20" cy="10" rx="4" ry="8"/><ellipse cx="30" cy="20" rx="8" ry="4"/><ellipse cx="20" cy="30" rx="4" ry="8"/><ellipse cx="10" cy="20" rx="8" ry="4"/><circle cx="20" cy="20" r="2"/>
children.quizClue: Four petal-like ovals arranged in a cross around a center dot.
children.quizWhy: Dogwood is known for its four showy petal-like bracts surrounding a small true flower cluster at the center.

families.name: Cornaceae
families.icon: <ellipse cx="20" cy="10" rx="4" ry="8"/><ellipse cx="30" cy="20" rx="8" ry="4"/><ellipse cx="20" cy="30" rx="4" ry="8"/><ellipse cx="10" cy="20" rx="8" ry="4"/><circle cx="20" cy="20" r="2"/>
families.trait: Small true flowers clustered tightly at the center, often surrounded by four large petal-like bracts that do the work of attracting pollinators.
families.differentia: The order's namesake family — its four large petal-like bracts surrounding a tight flower cluster are unlike Hydrangeaceae's ring of sterile florets around a fertile center.

funFacts.text: What looks like four large white or pink petals are actually modified leaves called bracts; the true flowers are the small yellow-green cluster at the center.
It blooms several weeks later than flowering dogwood and produces a raspberry-like, edible fruit that the earlier-blooming species lacks.
Native to East Asia, it was introduced to North America and Europe as an ornamental and has proven more resistant to dogwood anthracnose than the native flowering dogwood.

families.name: Hydrangeaceae
families.trait: Large rounded flower clusters combining small fertile flowers with larger sterile, showy ones around the outer edge; flower color in many species shifts with soil pH.
families.differentia: Distinguished from Cornaceae's bract-and-cluster look by a ring of enlarged sterile florets framing the true flowers, and by flower color that can shift with soil acidity.

funFacts.text: Flower color shifts between blue and pink depending on soil chemistry — acidic soil makes aluminum available to the plant, producing blue flowers, while alkaline soil locks aluminum away and yields pink ones.

children.desc: An early-diverging asterid order of shrubs and small trees bearing showy flower clusters, often relying on enlarged bracts or sterile outer florets rather than large true petals to attract pollinators.

children.name: Ericales
children.quizClue: A single urn- or bell-shaped outline, narrow at the top and swelling toward the bottom.
children.quizWhy: Blueberries, heather, and azaleas all share the order's signature urn- or bell-shaped fused petals.
children.desc: A structurally varied order, from acid-loving heathland shrubs to tropical timber trees, loosely bound by fused, urn- or bell-shaped petals and a preference for nutrient-poor soils.

families.name: Ericaceae
families.trait: Urn-shaped, fused petals; thrive in acidic soils, often partnered with mycorrhizal fungi.
families.differentia: The order's acid-soil specialist, with fused urn-shaped petals and obligate mycorrhizal partnerships not shared by the more generalist Theaceae or Primulaceae.

funFacts.text: Its blue color comes from anthocyanin pigments concentrated in a waxy surface bloom, which can be partly rubbed off by handling.

Ripe berries contain small internal air pockets, which is why growers flood bogs at harvest time — the berries float to the surface for easy collection, the source of the iconic floating-harvest image.
Grown in sandy, acidic bogs; for the wet harvest most people picture, the bogs are flooded and a machine beats the vines so the buoyant, air-pocketed berries float to the surface for collection.

In 401 BCE, the Greek general Xenophon recorded in his Anabasis that soldiers near Trebizond (modern Trabzon, Turkey) collapsed after eating local honey — an episode later explained by grayanotoxins concentrated from this rhododendron's nectar, one of the earliest documented accounts of a plant-derived poison identified centuries later by chemistry.
Blankets much of Scotland's moorland in purple bloom each late summer and is closely tied to Scottish cultural identity and traditional whisky and honey production.
Appears on the coat of arms of Madrid, depicted with a bear reaching up into its branches.
Its ripe fruit ferments slightly while still on the tree, and birds that eat large quantities can appear intoxicated.
Closely resembles blueberry but belongs to a different genus, distinguishable by ten large seeds inside each berry rather than blueberry's many tiny ones.

families.name: Theaceae
families.trait: Glossy evergreen leaves and showy, waxy-petaled flowers with a dense central boss of stamens.
families.differentia: Marked by glossy evergreen leaves and waxy, stamen-heavy flowers — showier and less soil-specific than the heath-loving Ericaceae.

funFacts.text: Green, black, oolong, and white tea all come from the same species — the differences come entirely from how the leaves are processed after picking, particularly how much they're allowed to oxidize.
Second only to water as the most widely consumed beverage on Earth.

Only the newest growth - the classic "two leaves and a bud" - is plucked by hand every week or two during the growing season; the same leaf can become green, oolong, or black tea depending entirely on how much it is withered, rolled, and oxidized afterward.
A long-favored ornamental in Japanese gardens, prized for glossy evergreen foliage and winter-to-spring blooms when little else flowers.
Native to wetland forests of the southeastern United States, often growing alongside cypress and bay swamps.

families.name: Primulaceae
families.trait: Low-growing herbs with basal leaf rosettes; five-petaled flowers radiating from a central eye.
families.differentia: Low herbaceous rosettes with radially symmetric five-petaled flowers, lacking the woody habit of Theaceae or Sapotaceae.

funFacts.text: One of the earliest wildflowers to bloom in the British spring, its name deriving from the Latin "prima rosa," or "first rose."
After flowering, its stems coil downward in a spiral to plant the seed pod directly into the soil beneath the parent plant.
Its small flowers close up in cloudy weather and by early afternoon, a trait that earned it the old English folk nickname "poor man's weatherglass."

families.name: Sapotaceae
families.trait: Milky latex sap throughout; tropical trees valued for edible fruit, oils, and natural rubber-like gums.
families.differentia: The only Ericales family here defined by milky latex sap running through leathery, tropical trees.

funFacts.text: Its milky latex, chicle, was the original base ingredient of chewing gum before synthetic substitutes largely replaced it in the mid-20th century.
Grows almost exclusively in a small region of southwestern Morocco, and its oil-rich seeds are traditionally hand-cracked by Berber women's cooperatives to produce argan oil.
In parts of Morocco, goats are famously photographed climbing into the tree's branches to browse its fruit.

Fruit is collected from the ground after falling; the nut inside the dried pulp is cracked by hand - a slow, labor-intensive step - and the kernels are pressed for oil, sometimes after light roasting for a more strongly flavored culinary grade.
Grows wild across the savanna belt of West and Central Africa; its fatty seed kernels are the source of shea butter.

Fallen fruit is gathered by hand from wild and semi-wild trees; the nut inside is dried, roasted, and pounded, then boiled and kneaded in water so the fat separates out and can be skimmed off as raw shea butter.

families.name: Actinidiaceae
families.trait: Woody, twining vines with fuzzy-skinned berries packed with tiny radiating seeds.
families.differentia: A woody, twining vine habit unique among this set — none of the other Ericales families here climb.

funFacts.text: Originally called the Chinese gooseberry; New Zealand growers renamed it "kiwifruit" in the 1950s for export marketing, after the country's iconic flightless bird.
Native to China, despite its strong modern association with New Zealand, where it became a major commercial crop in the 20th century.

families.name: Ebenaceae
families.trait: Dense, dark heartwood (the source of true ebony timber) or, in persimmon, sweet orange fruit that ripens from astringent to sweet; simple, often glossy leaves.
families.differentia: Unlike the acid-soil Ericaceae or milky-latex Sapotaceae, this family is defined by dense dark heartwood (ebony) or a fruit crowned with a papery calyx (persimmon).

funFacts.text: Produces some of the densest wood of any tree, dense enough to sink in water, which made it prized for fine furniture and musical instrument parts — and led to severe overharvesting of wild populations.
Unripe fruit is intensely astringent from high tannin content, causing a dry, puckering mouthfeel — the fruit becomes sweet and palatable only once fully ripened or specially treated.

families.name: Polemoniaceae
families.trait: Flat, five-lobed, star-shaped flowers fused into a narrow tube at the base, typically clustered into showy rounded heads; leaves often opposite and simple.
families.differentia: Distinguished from Primulaceae's single radiating bloom by flat five-lobed flowers clustered into showy rounded heads, and from Ericaceae's urn shape by an open, star-like corolla.

funFacts.text: Its name comes from the Greek word for "flame," a reference to the vivid color of its wild-type flowers.

Several of its most valuable crops - tea, blueberries, cranberries - all need distinctly acidic soil to thrive, a shared requirement traced back to a common ancestor rather than convergent coincidence.

children.name: Gentianales
children.quizClue: A five-pointed star shape radiating out from a center dot.
children.quizWhy: Coffee, milkweed, and gentians often have five-parted, star-shaped tubular flowers.

families.name: Apocynaceae
families.trait: Milky latex sap in stems and leaves; flowers with petals twisted or fused into a tube, often with an elaborate corona; many produce cardiac glycosides toxic to most animals but tolerated by specialist insects like monarch caterpillars.
families.differentia: Distinguished from Rubiaceae's four-parted tubular flowers by milky latex sap and a warty, silk-haired seed pod, a hallmark of milkweed and its dogbane relatives.

funFacts.text: The only food source for monarch butterfly caterpillars — the larvae sequester the plant's toxic cardenolide compounds in their own tissue, making both the caterpillar and adult butterfly distasteful to predators.
Its milky latex sap is mildly toxic and gives the plant its name.
Its tough stem fibers were twisted into cordage and textiles by Indigenous peoples across North America long before European contact.

families.name: Rubiaceae
families.icon: <path d="M20 34V16"/><ellipse cx="14" cy="14" rx="5" ry="8" transform="rotate(-20 14 14)"/><ellipse cx="26" cy="14" rx="5" ry="8" transform="rotate(20 26 14)"/><circle cx="16" cy="26" r="3"/><circle cx="24" cy="26" r="3"/>
families.trait: Opposite leaves joined at the base by a stipule; small, four- or five-lobed tubular flowers followed by fleshy berries, each containing two seeds.
families.differentia: The order's most economically important family here — opposite leaves with fused basal stipules and paired fleshy berries distinguish it from the milky, pod-bearing Apocynaceae.

funFacts.text: Popular legend credits an Ethiopian goatherd named Kaldi with discovering coffee's stimulating effects after noticing his goats grew energetic from eating the berries — a colorful story with no solid historical evidence behind it.
Native to the highlands of Ethiopia, and still grows wild there in forest understories today.
Ripe red cherries are hand-picked, then either dried whole in the sun or pulped and fermented in water to strip the fruit from the bean, which is then dried, hulled, and roasted.

children.desc: Mostly tropical trees, shrubs, and vines with opposite leaves and fused, tubular flower parts, spanning both milky-latex milkweeds and the world's coffee supply.

children.name: Boraginales
children.quizClue: Five small overlapping circles around a center dot — more delicate and compact than a rose-like bloom.
children.quizWhy: Forget-me-nots and borage have small, delicate five-petaled flowers, often blue or purple.

families.name: Boraginaceae
families.trait: Coiled flower clusters (cymes) that unfurl like a fiddlehead as they bloom; leaves and stems often bristly with rough hairs; five-petaled flowers, frequently blue.
families.differentia: The order's defining family — a distinctive coiled, unfurling flower cluster (scorpioid cyme) sets it apart from the flower arrangements of neighboring Lamiid orders.

funFacts.text: Its star-shaped blue flowers taste faintly of cucumber and are often used fresh as an edible garnish.
Its common name comes from a German legend about a knight who drowned after picking the flowers for his beloved, crying out "forget me not" as he was swept away.

children.desc: Herbs and shrubs with a distinctive coiled flower cluster that unfurls as it blooms, most familiar through garden borage and forget-me-nots.

children.name: Solanales
children.quizClue: A five-line star with an unusually large, prominent center circle.
children.quizWhy: Tomatoes, potatoes, and petunias have flowers with a prominent, cone-like cluster of stamens at the center.

families.name: Solanaceae
families.trait: Flowers with five fused petals forming a star or funnel shape around a prominent central cone of stamens; many species contain alkaloids (nicotine, solanine, capsaicin) ranging from toxic to intensely flavorful.
families.differentia: The order's namesake and largest family — a star-shaped flower with a prominent stamen cone, and alkaloid chemistry absent from the twining vines of Convolvulaceae.

funFacts.text: Domesticated in the Andes of South America thousands of years ago, from wild tuber-bearing relatives still found there today.
Its near-total dependence in 19th-century Ireland on a single vulnerable variety contributed to the Great Famine, after a potato blight destroyed harvests for years running.
Tubers exposed to light turn green and produce elevated solanine, a bitter, toxic compound — those green portions should be cut away before eating.

Grown from cut, sprouted tuber pieces called seed potatoes rather than true seed; soil is mounded up around the stems ("hilling") as they grow to keep developing tubers covered and free of sunlight-induced greening, then the tubers are dug up once the foliage dies back.
Domesticated in South and East Asia, unlike most of its Solanaceae relatives, which trace back to the Americas.
Native to the Americas, where Indigenous peoples cultivated and used it ceremonially long before European contact.
Naturally produces nicotine as an insect-deterrent chemical defense, one of the most potent naturally occurring plant alkaloids.

Leaves are hand-picked in stages from the bottom of the plant upward as they ripen, then cured for days to weeks - by air, fire, or heat depending on the style - which turns them from green to the familiar brown.

Nicknamed the "poison apple" in Europe for roughly two centuries after its introduction, largely because botanists noted its resemblance to toxic nightshade relatives. A popular modern story blames lead-leaching pewter plates for poisoning aristocrats who ate it, but food historians have found no documented cases supporting that specific claim.
Its heat is measured on the Scoville scale, originally based on how much a pepper extract had to be diluted before a human taste panel could no longer detect its burn.
Capsaicin evolved partly to deter mammals, whose grinding teeth would destroy the seeds, while birds — unaffected by the compound — pass the seeds intact, favoring bird-based seed dispersal.
Every part of the plant is highly toxic, containing tropane alkaloids that have historically been used — and misused — for their potent hallucinogenic and pain-relieving effects.
Its spiky seed pod, which splits open into four sections, gives the plant its "thorn apple" name.

Native to the Andes of South America, but marketed since the 1960s under the name "tamarillo" — coined in New Zealand, where it's the leading commercial grower, to distinguish it from the unrelated true tomato.
The tough, bitter skin is inedible and typically peeled after blanching the fruit in hot water; the tart flesh inside is eaten fresh, stewed, or made into chutneys and sauces.

Grown as a fast-maturing shrub or small tree that can fruit within its first year or two from seed; egg-shaped fruit is hand-picked once it reaches full color, since it doesn't ripen much further once removed from the plant.

Its major food crops (tomato, potato, eggplant, pepper) are almost always started indoors or in seedbeds and transplanted out as young plants rather than direct-seeded, since the family's tropical origins make them slow and unreliable to start in cool spring soil.

families.name: Convolvulaceae
families.trait: Twining or trailing vines with funnel-shaped flowers that typically open at dawn and wilt by midday; often exude a milky sap.
families.differentia: Distinguished from Solanaceae's star-shaped, stamen-coned flower by a smooth funnel-shaped bloom on a twining vine, and by lacking the order's characteristic alkaloids.

funFacts.text: Its flowers typically open at dawn and close by early afternoon, giving the plant its common name.
A staple leafy green across Southeast Asian cooking, grown both floating on water and in flooded fields.

children.desc: Herbs and vines producing some of the world's most important food crops and a few of its most potent alkaloids, spanning the nightshades and the twining morning-glory vines.

funFacts.text: Nightshades (Solanaceae) as a group produce a wide range of alkaloids — some, like the nicotine in tobacco and solanine in green potato skin, are toxic, while others define the family's most valuable food crops.

children.name: Lamiales
children.icon: <rect x="14" y="6" width="4" height="28"/><rect x="22" y="6" width="4" height="28"/><ellipse cx="16" cy="14" rx="7" ry="4"/><ellipse cx="24" cy="24" rx="7" ry="4"/>
children.quizClue: Two vertical bars flanked by a pair of small oval blooms, like a square-stemmed mint sprig.
children.quizWhy: Mint, sage, and lavender are known for square stems and two-lipped (bilabiate) tubular flowers.
children.desc: Mostly herbs and shrubs with fused, often two-lipped (bilabiate) flowers and opposite leaves; square stems and aromatic oils recur across several families.

families.name: Lamiaceae
families.icon: <rect x="14" y="6" width="4" height="28"/><rect x="22" y="6" width="4" height="28"/><ellipse cx="16" cy="14" rx="7" ry="4"/><ellipse cx="24" cy="24" rx="7" ry="4"/>
families.trait: Square stems, opposite aromatic leaves rich in essential oils, and two-lipped tubular flowers.
families.differentia: The only family in this order with square stems and paired opposite leaves both saturated in aromatic oil — Oleaceae and Plantaginaceae lack the square-stem trait entirely.

funFacts.text: Its genus name, Salvia, comes from the Latin salvere, "to save" or "to heal," reflecting its long history as a medicinal herb.
Central to Italian cuisine, most famously as the base of pesto alla genovese.
Its name likely derives from the Latin lavare, "to wash," reflecting its long use in Roman bathing and laundry practices.

Whole flower spikes are cut in mid-summer once about half the buds on a stem have opened, then either dried in bundles or distilled almost immediately, since essential oil content drops the longer cut stems sit.
A naturally occurring hybrid of watermint and spearmint; it's sterile and produces little viable seed, so it's propagated almost entirely through cuttings and root division.

Reclassified from its own genus, Rosmarinus, into Salvia after genetic studies showed it was nested within that genus — a reminder that even long-familiar culinary herbs get renamed as DNA evidence updates classification.
Comes in green and red-purple varieties, both widely used across Japanese and Korean cuisine — red shiso is also used to dye pickled plums (umeboshi) their characteristic color.

families.name: Oleaceae
families.trait: Opposite leaves (often paired leaflets); four-petaled flowers, many wind- or insect-pollinated trees.
families.differentia: Woody where most Lamiales relatives are herbaceous; four-petaled flowers and paired leaflets mark it apart from the two-lipped blooms typical elsewhere in the order.

funFacts.text: Cultivated across the Mediterranean for at least 6,000 years, with some individual trees estimated to be over a thousand years old and still bearing fruit.

Trees are pruned hard each year to an open shape that lets light reach the fruit; olives are picked (by hand, rake, or mechanical shaker) while still green for a sharper oil or fully ripe and black for a milder one, then pressed within hours to avoid spoilage.
Its genus name comes from the Greek word for "pipe," a reference to the hollow stems once used to make simple flutes.
Long the preferred wood for baseball bats, valued for its strength-to-weight ratio and flexibility.
North American ash populations have been devastated since the 2000s by the emerald ash borer, an invasive beetle that has killed hundreds of millions of trees.
Named after Scottish botanist William Forsyth; its bright yellow blooms are one of the earliest and most recognizable signs of spring in temperate gardens.
Its flowers are used to scent jasmine tea, traditionally made by layering fresh blossoms with tea leaves overnight so the leaves absorb the fragrance.

families.name: Plantaginaceae
families.trait: Diverse habit from lawn weeds to garden ornamentals, united by asymmetric, often spurred flowers.
families.differentia: United by asymmetric, often spurred flowers rather than the strict bilabiate (two-lipped) shape seen in Lamiaceae, spanning everything from lawn weeds to foxgloves.

funFacts.text: English physician William Withering learned of a folk remedy for "dropsy" (fluid retention from heart failure) from a Shropshire herbalist in 1775, traced its effectiveness to foxglove, and after a decade of careful case studies published "An Account of the Foxglove" in 1785 — establishing digitalis as a heart medication still used in modified form today.
Highly toxic in raw form; the same compounds that make it medicinally valuable in controlled doses can be fatal if the plant is eaten directly.
Its dried seed pods split open in a pattern that resembles a small skull, a resemblance that has made them popular in Halloween-themed floral displays.

Traditionally chewed or crushed into a poultice for minor cuts and insect stings in Anglo-Saxon England — one of the nine sacred herbs named in the Old English "Nine Herbs Charm" — and later adopted by Indigenous peoples in North America, who called it "white man's footprint" for how closely it tracked European settlement.
Unrelated to the banana-like plantain fruit — the two simply share an English common name.
The husk surrounding its tiny seeds swells into a gel when mixed with water, which is why it is widely used as a natural dietary fiber supplement.

families.name: Bignoniaceae
families.trait: Large, showy trumpet-shaped flowers; many climbing lianas or flowering trees of warm climates.
families.differentia: Defined by unusually large, trumpet-shaped flowers and a climbing or tree habit not found among the smaller-flowered herbs of Lamiaceae or Verbenaceae.

funFacts.text: Its leaves are the sole food source of catalpa sphinx moth caterpillars, prized by anglers as fish bait in parts of the southeastern U.S.
Its long tubular orange-red flowers are a favorite nectar source for hummingbirds, which can reach nectar that most insects cannot.
Native to South America but planted so extensively as a street tree in cities like Pretoria, Los Angeles, and Lisbon that its vivid purple spring bloom has become a signature seasonal event in each.

families.name: Verbenaceae
families.trait: Small flowers clustered in dense spikes; leaves often rough-textured, some yield durable timber.
families.differentia: Similar square stems to Lamiaceae, but flowers are packed into dense spikes rather than paired whorls, and several members are timber trees rather than herbs.

funFacts.text: Its leaves carry an intense lemon fragrance from citral and are steeped for herbal tea across South America and the Mediterranean.
Called "herba sacra" by the ancient Romans, who used it in purification rituals and considered it sacred.
Contains natural oils that make its timber highly resistant to rot, warping, and insects even without chemical treatment, prized for centuries in shipbuilding and outdoor furniture.

families.name: Pedaliaceae
families.trait: Sticky, mucilage-covered capsules split open at maturity to release small, oil-rich seeds; opposite leaves often glandular-hairy.
families.differentia: The order's oilseed specialist — small pods packed with tiny oil-rich seeds distinguish it from the square-stemmed herbs of Lamiaceae and the woody Oleaceae.

funFacts.text: One of the oldest oilseed crops cultivated by humans, with evidence of use dating back over 5,000 years.
Its seed pods burst open abruptly when fully dry — very likely the origin of the phrase "open sesame" from One Thousand and One Nights.

Harvested just as the lowest seed pods begin to split, since fully ripe pods shatter and scatter seed on their own; cut plants are stacked upright to finish drying before threshing shakes the seed loose.

families.name: Paulowniaceae
families.trait: Large heart-shaped leaves and showy, upright clusters of tubular purple flowers blooming before the leaves emerge; among the fastest-growing hardwood trees known.
families.differentia: The order's fastest-growing tree — large heart-shaped leaves and an upright spike of purple tubular flowers set it apart from the smaller herbs and shrubs typical of Lamiales.

funFacts.text: One of the fastest-growing trees in the world, capable of adding several meters of height in a single growing season.
In traditional Japanese custom, a paulownia tree was sometimes planted when a daughter was born, then harvested and carved into furniture for her dowry chest when she came of age.

Many of this order's culinary herbs (basil, mint, sage) are cut back hard and repeatedly through the season, which delays flowering and keeps the plant producing the tender new growth that carries the most flavor and aromatic oil.

children.name: Aquifoliales
children.quizClue: A pointed leaf shape with a single berry hanging beneath it.
children.quizWhy: Holly is instantly recognizable by its pointed leaves and bright red berries.

families.name: Aquifoliaceae
families.trait: Simple, often spiny-toothed evergreen leaves; small white flowers followed by bright, berry-like drupes; several species (mate, guayusa) are brewed into caffeinated infusions.
families.differentia: The order's sole family — every Aquifoliales species tagged here, ornamental holly and caffeinated mate alike, belongs to the single genus Ilex.

funFacts.text: Its evergreen leaves and red winter berries made it a symbol of life persisting through winter in pre-Christian European tradition, later absorbed into Christmas decoration.
The bright red berries are mildly toxic to humans if eaten in quantity, though many birds rely on them as a winter food source.
Brewed into mate, a caffeinated infusion central to social life across Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, and southern Brazil, traditionally sipped through a metal straw from a shared gourd.

children.desc: A single-genus order — every species here, ornamental holly and caffeinated mate alike, belongs to Ilex.

children.name: Apiales
children.quizClue: An umbrella-like spray of lines ending in small dots, like an umbel of tiny flowers.
children.quizWhy: Carrots, dill, and parsley all produce their tiny flowers in umbrella-shaped clusters called umbels.

families.name: Apiaceae
families.trait: Tiny five-petaled flowers clustered into umbrella-shaped compound umbels; hollow, ridged stems and finely divided, aromatic leaves; many produce essential oils used as spices.
families.differentia: The order's namesake and dominant family — umbrella-shaped flower clusters (umbels) on hollow ridged stems distinguish nearly every Apiales species here from the woody Araliaceae.

funFacts.text: Every part is used in cooking — the bulb, stalks, feathery leaves, and seeds all have distinct culinary uses across Mediterranean cuisine.
One of the most widely used spices worldwide, foundational to Indian, Middle Eastern, and Mexican cuisines alike.
Sweetens noticeably after exposure to frost, as cold triggers the root to convert stored starches into sugars.
Both its feathery leaves and its seeds are used in cooking, with distinctly different flavors — fresh and grassy from the leaves, warmer and more pungent from the seeds.

Shares its dominant licorice-like flavor compound, anethole, with several unrelated plants like fennel and star anise, which is why they're often confused despite belonging to entirely different families.
Used in ancient Greece to crown victors at the Isthmian Games, well before it became a common culinary herb.

Wild carrot roots are thin, pale, and bitter; the familiar large orange root is the result of centuries of selective breeding, with orange varieties becoming dominant in the Netherlands around the 17th century.
Direct-seeded rather than transplanted, since the taproot doesn't recover well from disturbance; thinned early to give remaining roots room, then pulled once the shoulders reach full size.
Its long fibrous stalks are leaf petioles, not stems — the plant's actual stem is a short, compact structure at the base.

A slow starter usually begun indoors and transplanted out; stalks are often blanched by mounding soil or wrapping the base to block light and reduce bitterness, then the whole head is cut at the base at harvest.

families.name: Araliaceae
families.trait: Often woody shrubs, trees, or vines with palmately compound leaves; small flowers in umbel-like clusters, and in ginseng, a slow-growing forked root prized in traditional medicine.
families.differentia: The order's only woody family here — distinguished from Apiaceae's herbaceous umbels by a shrub or tree habit and, in ginseng, a slow-growing forked taproot.

funFacts.text: Used in traditional East Asian medicine for centuries as a general tonic, though rigorous clinical evidence for many of its purported benefits remains limited.
Its genus name, Panax, comes from the Greek for "all-heal," reflecting the wide range of traditional uses attributed to the root.

children.desc: Aromatic herbs (and a few woody outliers) known for umbrella-shaped flower clusters and essential oils, supplying much of the world's savory spice cabinet.

funFacts.text: Nearly every member of the carrot family produces distinctive umbrella-shaped flower clusters (umbels) and aromatic essential oils, making it a rich source of both root vegetables and culinary spices.

children.name: Dipsacales
children.quizClue: Two curved trumpet shapes branching together from one stem, like paired honeysuckle blooms.
children.quizWhy: Honeysuckle produces paired tubular flowers that grow directly from the same point on the stem.

families.name: Caprifoliaceae
families.trait: Paired, often fragrant tubular flowers with fused petals opening into flaring lobes; many are climbing or scrambling shrubs, though the family (broadened by DNA evidence) also includes the low herbaceous valerian.
families.differentia: Distinguished from Adoxaceae's flat-topped flower clusters by paired, fused tubular flowers and (in honeysuckle) a climbing, twining habit.

funFacts.text: Its tubular, fragrant flowers, most intensely scented at night, are shaped to suit long-tongued moths and hummingbirds rather than typical bees.
Its root has a long history of use as an herbal sleep aid and mild sedative, with a distinctively strong, musky smell that many people find unpleasant despite its calming reputation.
Its scent is intensely attractive to domestic cats, similar to catnip, and is sometimes used in cat toys for that reason.

families.name: Adoxaceae
families.trait: Small white flowers packed into broad, flat-topped clusters (corymbs), followed by clusters of small dark berries; compound, opposite leaves.
families.differentia: The order's flat-topped bloomer — broad clusters of tiny white flowers set it apart from Caprifoliaceae's larger, paired tubular blooms.

funFacts.text: Its flowers are used to make elderflower cordial and liqueur, while its cooked berries go into syrups and jams.
Raw or unripe berries, along with the leaves, stems, and seeds, contain cyanogenic compounds and can cause nausea — cooking neutralizes them, which is why elderberry is always used cooked, not raw.

children.desc: Shrubs, vines, and herbs of the northern temperate zone bearing clustered tubular or flat-topped flowers, spanning ornamental honeysuckle, medicinal valerian, and elderflower.

children.name: Asterales
children.quizClue: A center disc ringed by many thin radiating lines — the most literal daisy shape in the set.
children.quizWhy: Daisies and sunflowers are composite flowers — what looks like one bloom is really a disc of many tiny flowers ringed by petal-like rays.

families.name: Asteraceae
families.trait: Flower heads that are actually dense clusters of many tiny florets packed onto a single receptacle, surrounded by protective bracts, giving the appearance of one large bloom; among the largest of all flowering-plant families.
families.differentia: The order's sole family and one of the two largest plant families on Earth — what looks like a single flower is really a composite head of dozens to hundreds of tiny florets.

funFacts.text: The edible part is an unopened flower bud — if left to bloom, it opens into a large, thistle-like purple flower.

Grown as a perennial from root divisions or seed; the edible part is the immature flower bud, hand-cut with a length of stem while its scales are still tight, since an opened bud turns tough and inedible.
Its hooked seed burrs, which cling to fur and clothing, are widely credited with inspiring the invention of Velcro in the 1940s.
Also called Jerusalem artichoke, despite having no connection to Jerusalem or true artichokes — it's actually a species of sunflower grown for its edible tuber.
Young sunflower buds track the sun's movement across the sky each day, a behavior called heliotropism, but mature flowers stop moving and generally settle facing east.
Domesticated by Indigenous peoples in North America long before Europeans encountered it.

Direct-seeded in spring; the flower heads are left to dry in the field until the back turns brown and the seeds rattle loose, then combine-harvested and the seed pressed for oil or hulled for snacking.
One of the most widely consumed herbal teas, traditionally used to promote relaxation and settle digestion.
Its roasted, ground root has long been used as a coffee substitute or additive, especially popular in parts of the American South and Louisiana.
Roots are dug up in autumn, then dried and roasted until dark and brittle, at which point they're ground into a bitter, caffeine-free substitute for or additive to coffee.
Its seed head's parachute-like structures allow individual seeds to travel long distances on the wind, an efficient dispersal strategy that also makes it a notoriously persistent lawn weed.
Every part is edible — the leaves in salads, the flowers in wine or fritters, and the roasted root as a coffee substitute.
Central to Mexico's Día de los Muertos celebrations, where its bright orange flowers are believed to guide spirits back to visit the living with their scent and color.
The imperial emblem of Japan, where the throne is traditionally referred to as the Chrysanthemum Throne.
Its petals are steeped for a traditional East Asian tea, and certain varieties are eaten as a leafy vegetable.
What looks like a single flower is actually a composite head of two floret types: yellow disc florets in the center and white ray florets forming the "petals."

Its milky sap, released when the stem is cut, contains a mild sedative compound called lactucarium, which gave rise to its old nickname "lettuce opium" — though the effect from eating lettuce is negligible.
Direct-seeded or transplanted as seedlings; leaf types are cut repeatedly as outer leaves mature, while head types are cut once at the base when the head feels firm.
Traditionally used as an herbal remedy for headaches and migraines, a use with some modern research support though results remain mixed.

children.desc: The daisy order — composite flower heads built from many tiny florets crowded onto a single receptacle, spanning garden ornamentals, salad greens, and the towering sunflower.

funFacts.text: The daisy family's "flowers" are actually flower heads made of many tiny individual florets packed together — a sunflower's yellow "petals" and central disc are each composed of dozens to hundreds of separate flowers.
